units.la: DULCE & amabile est nomen Amicitiæ & Concordiæ: res verò ipsa dulcissima longeq; jucundissima: quippe quæ omnis chori ethnici coryphæo & tanquam antistiti PLatoni συμφωνίαν νοημάτων κ) ὑπολημμάτων: ὁμόνοιαν ὑπὲρ καλῶν κ) δικαίων: κοινωνίαν βίυ μετ' εὐνοίας, κ) ἓ εὖ ποιῆσαι καὶ παθεῖν, κ) τῶν ὄντων ἁπάντων: animorum, studiorum & sententiarum tanquam concentum: summam de justis & honestis consensionem: beneficiorum & affectionum, & omnium deniq; rerum, quarum communicatio esse potest, communitatem ab omni invidia liberam complectatur: cujus quidem fundamentum & primaria causa αὐτόφιλον κ) πρῶτον φίλον Deus, efficax animorum veluti ψυχαγωγὸς atq; conciliator: ζυγαῖπον verò, & quidem id suo modo potentissimum, ὁμοιότης & οἰκειότης morum similitudo & cognatio, non nisi é bonis viris elucens, quibus omnis vita est εὐάρμοστος, & secum præclarè consentiens.
units.tr: The name of friendship and concord is sweet and lovable, but the thing itself is most sweet and by far most pleasant. Plato, the leader and, as it were, the chief of the whole pagan chorus, describes it as an agreement of thoughts and opinions [συμφωνίαν νοημάτων καὶ ὑπολήψεων], a concord about what is noble and just [ὁμόνοιαν ὑπὲρ καλῶν καὶ δικαίων], a partnership of life with goodwill, and of doing and suffering good [κοινωνίαν βίου μετ' εὐνοίας, καὶ τὸ εὖ ποιῆσαι καὶ παθεῖν], and of all existing things [καὶ τῶν ὄντων ἁπάντων]. It is a kind of concert of minds, pursuits and opinions: a broad agreement about what is just and honourable, and a community, free from all envy, of benefits and affections, and finally of all the things which can be shared. Its foundation and primary cause is God, who is the friend of himself and the first friend [αὐτόφιλον καὶ πρῶτον φίλον], the efficient guide and uniter of minds, as it were. The yoke that joins them, and in its own way the most powerful, is the similarity and kinship of character [ὁμοιότης καὶ οἰκειότης], which shines forth only among good men, whose whole life is well-harmonised and agrees splendidly with itself [εὐάρμοστος].

units.la: Hæc harmonia non δημώδης popularis, sed μεγίστης illius Musicæ Socraticæ, hoc est Ethicæ, pars est insignis, qua suavior, concinnior & melior nec excogitari, nec sensu percipi potest. Itaq; Philosophus Hermeam, Coriscum, Erastum, viros eximios, gravissimé hortatur, ut in eam rem certatim incumbant, ut concordibus animis in unum quen-dam unius amicitiæ complexum, unamq; communitatem mutuis ne-xibus coalescant. Et in Dialogis suis sapientissimis passim κοινωνίαν καὶ συμπαλοχὴν[?] hanc, & concordem germanitatem perquam magnificé & splendidissimis verbis commendat. Quæ ut olim magna cum volupta-te mente complexus sum: sic quoties, CASPAR PEVCERE, vir eximie, memoria & cogitatione mecum repeto atq; recolligo: toties opti-morum quondam Procerum & Doctorum, adeoq; pulcerrimi cœtus, & universæ Reipubl. Scholasticæ in Academia Witebergensi status memoria, non animo modo, sed prope oculis meis obversatur. Etenim ea habuit inde usq; ab initio, suo quodam peculiari fato, & Dei perbe-nigno concessu, cum alia multa singularia, antequam alvei illius mi-serè perturbarentur & disjicerentur, tum vero hoc maximè, quod in docetibus τὸ ὅμοιον καὶ ξύμφωνον[?] illud semper fuit, hoc est, voluntatum inter eos consensio, arctissima animorum colligatio, copulatioq; in Deo, & ὁμοδοξία[?]: auditorum vero atq; discentium ea erga præceptores suos & erga se mutuo affectio, ut ubicunq; postea, etiam multorum annorum spatio decurso, vel cōgressi sunt superioribus annis, vel etiamnum conveniunt priores illi Witebergenses, non nisi cum summa animi lætitia inter se amare & complecti cernas. Fuit & admirabilis pené omnium, qui vel docuerunt, vel didicerunt in ea Schola, ut in alijs, ita & in sermonis genere & charactere dicendi, una tanquam Musica, hoc est congruentia & similitudo. Perfecit id sua dexteritate, sapien-tia, suavitate vocis, & penna bonitate, quibus ornatus & auctorita-te, qua armatus fuit à Deo, pené inimitabili, MAGnus[?] ille Philippus Melanchthon, socer tuus, beatissimæ memoriæ: Qui fuit feré primus & communis præceptor, atq; ceu οἰκοδεσπότης[?], & magister ac instaurator cum omnium aliarum doctrinarum in Germania, tum vero etiam studiorum eloquentiæ, quæ ipse & magno conatu excitabat & propagabat, bene favente Deo, felicissimè: cum quidem & primis & posteri-oribus temporibus solus feré adornaret ac scriberet, quæ proponebantur aut recitabantur publicè vel ab ipso, vel ab alijs, gravissimæ doctrinæ & commonefactionis omnia: aut alios in scriptione eruditis & piis subjectionibus rerum & luminum insignium sedulo adjuvaret. Hinc adeò factum, ut pulcra omnium inter se esset æquabilitas, hoc est, ut ad normam & exemplum expressionemq; virtutum summi artificis componerent ac referrent se in Schola cæteri omnes, cùm & conjungeret omnes & copularet inter se arte mira, Ethica seu concinnitate morum dulci, Philosophia sobria, Theologia sancta, patientia, candore, pietate, lenitate & bonitate divina. Hæc enim decora cùm in eo essent illustriora & conspectiora, quasi incantationis cujusdam efficaciam habebant, (ut cum Platone iterum loquar) ut mirabiles sui amores in omnium animis excitarent, & pulchritudo illorum ad imitationem impelleret. Nulla enim re homo bonos magis ad se attrahit & allicit, aut voluntates inter se conciliat, quàm splendore veræ virtutis. Sic ergo Philomela illa Germaniæ, & oris & manus ac calami plectro, canente, præcinente, succinente, modos faciente & regente, Leucoreis erat una manus, vox una, cor unum: & quid multa? una & concors Musica. Nec vel aurum splendidum, vel adamas [illegible, ~10 letters] ita coruscat in hominum oculis (liceat enim rursus augustè cum Platone loqui) atq; fulgebat Melanchthoniorum, hoc est, bonorum ὁμοφρόνων [?] νόησις, mens consentiens. Cùm verò sanctè & beatè è specula jam decessisset heroicus ille excubitor atq; custos, qui pervigilans in communi studio indefesso benefaciebat omnibus: tota domus cœpit tunc onus esse tuum. Nam qui & in gubernatione rectorum studiorum, & in conservanda ac fulcienda Republica Scholastica utilissimè quasi succederet, inventus tu es & habitus ferè solus. Et illa quidem, ut jam dudum in intelligentium virorum animis confirmata insederat, ita vera omninò de te existimatio fuit, ut cui [illegible, ~9 letters] liciter responderint: quandoquidem beata illius anima personam quasi, cum magna laude & admiratione sustinens, præterquàm quòd fidelis & prudens eras ἐξεδιώκτης [?], corporis & tanquam συνήμα- scholastici harmoniam & conjunctionem singulari Dei munere, & præ& præclara tua virtute tuebaris, & Scholæ res multis modis amplifi-cabas: donec tandem fatalis illa machina, & horum temporum infe-licitas mutationem rebus & locis attulit magnam, adeoq; te publicæ luci & hominum oculis eripuit, non sine ingenti dolore, & veris gemi-tibus piorum & bonorum aliquot annis desideratum. Cum igitur, ut miraculum divinæ misericordiæ (id enim te esse vere scribis) & alter Josephus, ex tenebris longis & ambagibus longis in solem ac lucem se-nex, heroico climactere LXIII. jam superato, & animo & corpore be-nè valente, reductus, nuper hic in comitatu aulico Illustrissimorum Principum, laudatissimæ & antiquissimæ familiæ Ascaniæ nobis quo-que tandem reddereris [?], lætitia perfusi sumus incredibili: cùm nos, qui partim Scholæ Witebergensis fuimus aliquando alumni, partim præterea tibi amicitia vel cognationis necessitudine intimè juncti, par-tim in docendo etiam tandem Collegæ: tum verò alii quoq; magnifici & nobilissimi viri, & Professores eximii, qui celebritate nominis tui, rerumq; à te piè & constanter gestarum, qui fama & prædicatione de tuis ornamentis & præclaris erga rempublicam meritis, & perpetuò duraturis ingenii tui monumentis moti, conspectum tuum avidissimè eruditorum sermonum caussa jamdudum expetebant. Mox verò tum omnes unà etiam dolebamus, quod vix incoata de multis publicis in primis & privatis rebus dulcissima colloquia interrumpebat, nobisq; auferebat abitus tuus, quo mox altero die, postquam venisti, à comple-xu nostro rursus avellebare, tuam aulam illustrem sequens, lateriq; ceu custos animi & corporis junctus adolescentibus Principibus, quos ut antiquissima & laudatissima est eorum familia, ita audimus verè an-tiquæ & præclaræ virtutis ac pietatis præbere atq; ostendere de se spem & expectationem certam omnibus, eamq; ut larga sua gratia firmam ac ratam velit esse Deus, qui unus dat salutem Regibus, optamus. Te quoq; citius hinc, quàm vellemus à nobis abductum, animis, cùm cor-poribus nequeamus, & votis nostris piè ad Deum pro te conceptis, & quibuscunq; possumus officij significationibus prosequimur. Quare ut Principes Illustrissimi Hassiæ, veri & pii hoc ferreo seculo Ecclesiæ nutritores, συνεργός[?], & Domini nostri benignissimi, te clementissima af-sectione ac humanitate in hac gente sua & terra sunt complexi: ita nobis quoq; quàm gratus & optatus fueris in schola hospes, judicavi publicè ostendendum. Nam cùm inter cætera, cum significatione benevolétiæ studii, & officij singularis, ad solennem etiam publicæ promotio-nis nostræ actum mane accesseris, eo ipso die, quo mox à prandio, quod in tuum honorem Academia paraverat, discedens nobis bené preca-baris: atq; publici nostri congressus actus de consilio optimorum viro-rum edendus esset, cui eum potius ac libentius inscriberem, quàm tibi, non invenio quenquam. Quod enim de isto argumento, in quo oratio mea versata est, tenere mihi videor, judico tibi nonnulla ex parte de-beri, & cum fœnore tibi reddendum, quod à te acceptum tuli, qui in disputatione publica habita Anno 1571, cui R. & Cl. vir Caspar Cruci-ger Theologiæ Doctor, magna cum laude præsidebat, gravissimè & doctissimè ex ipso fundamento dissereres adversus πεϱιτῶν ἐντϱωμάτα[?] Βλαχικὰ: sicut sanè longo tempore Flacianæ striges primùm quidem Melanchthoni socero tuo, postea & tibi feralis suo cantu obstrepentes, inq; vos in primis fato quodam, Deo puniente peccata hominum, incurrentes, ut in urbibus & pectoribus multorum, ita & in Academia ad Albim nidificare, & pullos suos degeneres eniti, & volucres obscœnas excludere concupiverunt: é quibus formæ maximè abhorrentis sunt, Homo brutus, bestialis, truncus: Corruptio hominis talis, qualis est transmutatio substantiæ Physica in aliam & novam: Caro alterius seu diversæ speciei: Conversio & impressio imaginis Dei, ac infusio gratiæ Spiritus divini momentanea & violenta in hominem, ut in Urceolos vacuos: Homo lapsus αὐθαμαρτησία[?], id est, peccatum ipsum & opus Diaboli: quibus & portentosa Theologia inducitur: (quæ non habet testimonium spiritualis experientiæ piorum in cordibus) & homo ex homine exuitur: & Physica cum Theologicis, naturalia cum voluntariis miscentur: & οὐσία[?] rei cum πάθει[?] ipsis confunditur: quæ non discernere est ἀπαιδευσία[?] tenebris sese & alios involvere, ne quid dicam gravius. Habeo & alias non prorsus nullo numero causas meæ hujus θεσιφω-[?] μεσοφωνήσεως, quas nunc mitto, quód, ne epistola modum excedat, ad extrema properem. Talis est, praestantissime vir, vera Ecclesia: coetus piorum, saepe etiam paucorum, consentiens de vera doctrina, & simul etiam in dissimilia longoq; intervallo disjuncta κλίματα sparsus, recte invocans Deum, & conjunctionis piae amans, etsi non sit inclusus, ut multi putant, intra unius atq; alterius opidi moenia, aut etiam unius gentis circumscriptus limitibus: defensionem deniq; habens à Deo, etsi fert dominationem & clamores hypocritarum & Sycophantarum, af-flantq; eam fumi atq; flatus Typhonū, qui audacissime cominiscuntur, disseminant, & propagant opiniones dissimiles, convitiaq; tetra projiciunt in Deum & homines. Quare ut hoc qualecunq; mei μνημόσυνον, & conjunctionis tum illius, quae solet atq; consuevit esse, ut dixi initio, in-ter γνώσεως Academiae Witebergensis homines, tum hujus, quae mihi est tecum in Christo, Ecclesiae capite, adeoq; observantiae erga te meae te-stimonium, amáter à me accipias, & hanc meam compellationem, au-daciusculam fortasse, gratā tibi acceptamq; esse patiaris, humaniter pe-to. Simul etiam oro, ut, si per occupationes instaurandarū rursus rerū quarundam, doctrinarū & historiarum utilium ac necessariarum, haec nostra (quae quidem multitudine Scholasticarum θεολογικῶν[?] μαθηματῶν[?] aliarum penè obruto non fas fuit ad tenue elimare) inspicere licebit, de tuo judicio & censura diserte significare ne graveris: cum quidem antea quoq; & benevolentia tua adjutus ac recreatus, & judicio atq; candore tuo sincero delectatus sim. Latabor igitur, si & deinceps, quid sentias aut probes, mihi liberè & liberaliter ostenderis. Deum autem fontem omnis cognitionis & doctrinae toto pectore oro, ut veram lucem & intellectum Philosophiae & Theologiae sobriae in multis accendat, atq; in nobis magis magisq; confirmet: faciatq; ut diu adhuc in cursu inter honestissimos placidiore & tranquilliore, inq; medicationibus, quae prosunt Principibus, & multorum hominum vitae, Ecclesiae, & communibus omnis generis eruditae, piae, & sincerae doctrinae studiis servire possis. Bene & feliciter vale. Marpurg. ex Museo nostro, Idibus Augusti, Anno Servatoris 1588.
units.tr: This harmony is not the popular kind, but a notable part of that great Socratic music, that is, of ethics. Nothing sweeter, more harmonious, or better can be conceived or perceived by the senses. So the Philosopher earnestly urges Hermeas, Coriscus, and Erastus, outstanding men, to strive eagerly for this, so that with united minds they may grow together into one embrace of friendship and one fellowship bound by mutual ties. And in his most wise Dialogues he commends this fellowship [κοινωνίαν] and companionship [συμπαλοχὴν], and this agreeable brotherhood, everywhere and in the most splendid and magnificent words. As I once embraced these things with great delight, so, whenever, distinguished CASPAR PEUCER, I recall and gather them again in memory and thought with you, the image of the former assembly of the best leaders and teachers, of that most beautiful company, and of the whole scholarly commonwealth at the Academy of Wittenberg, rises before my mind and almost before my eyes. For from the beginning, by a certain peculiar fate and by God's most gracious gift, that school had many singular features before its channel was wretchedly disturbed and broken up. Above all, this was so: among its teachers there was always that same agreement [τὸ ὅμοιον καὶ ξύμφωνον], that is, a consensus of wills, a very close binding of minds, and a joining together in God, and one [ὁμοδοξία] shared opinion. Among the hearers and learners there was such affection toward their teachers and toward one another that wherever those former Wittenbergers have met, even after many years have passed, or still meet in these recent years, you see them loving and embracing one another with the greatest joy of mind. There was also, among almost all who taught or learned in that school, a wonderful likeness in their manner of speaking and style of writing, as in one music, that is, a harmony and similarity. This was brought about by his skill, wisdom, sweetness of voice, and goodness of pen, and by the almost inimitable authority and gifts with which God had armed that great Philip Melanchthon, your father-in-law, of most blessed memory. He was almost the first and common teacher, and as a good householder [οἰκοδεσπότης], the master and restorer of all other learning in Germany, and above all of the study of eloquence, which he himself, with great effort and with God's favour, most successfully aroused and spread. In the early and later times he almost alone prepared and wrote whatever was proposed or read publicly, either by himself or by others, all of the most serious teaching and admonition, or he diligently helped others in writing learned and pious treatises on notable matters and lights. Hence it came about that there was a fine evenness among them all: all the rest arranged and conformed themselves in the school to the rule and pattern and expression of the virtues of the supreme Artificer, since he joined and bound them all together with wonderful art: sweet ethics or the harmony of good morals, sober philosophy, holy theology, patience, candour, piety, gentleness, and divine goodness. For these graces shone and were most visible in him, and they had a kind of power of enchantment (to speak again with Plato) so that they stirred up wonderful loves in the minds of all, and their beauty drove men to imitate them. For nothing draws and attracts good men to itself, or unites wills with one another, more than the brightness of true virtue. Thus that Philomela of Germany, with her mouth, hand, and pen as a plectrum, sang, led the chorus, sang in response, made and directed the measures; with Leucorean ... there was one hand, one voice, one heart, and why say more? one harmonious music. Nor does gold or diamond [illegible] sparkle so in men's eyes (for I may again speak nobly with Plato) as the understanding of the Melanchthonians, that is, of good men of one mind, a consenting mind. But when that heroic sentinel and guardian, who kept watch and worked without wearying for the common good for the benefit of all, had blessedly and holily departed from his post, then the whole house began to be your burden. For you were found and regarded almost alone as the one who would succeed, most usefully, in governing the studies and in preserving and supporting the scholastic commonwealth. That was indeed firmly fixed in the minds of discerning men, and the true opinion of you was such that [illegible] they answered accordingly. For since his blessed soul, you were, with great praise and admiration, as it were sustaining his role; besides being a faithful and prudent [ἐξεδιώκτης] steward, you protected the harmony and union of the body and of the school, which is the singular gift of God, by your distinguished virtue, and you increased the affairs of the school in many ways, until at last that fatal machine and the unhappiness of these times brought a great change to affairs and places, and tore you away from public light and from the eyes of men, not without great grief and true sighs of some pious and good men, who missed you for several years. Therefore, when you, a miracle of divine mercy (for so you truly write yourself) and a second Joseph, had been brought back from long darkness and long wanderings into the sun and light, an old man, now past the heroic climacteric of sixty-three years, and in good health of mind and body, and recently here in the court retinue of the most illustrious princes of the most praised and ancient house of Anhalt, and finally given back to us, we were filled with incredible joy. For we, some of whom were once pupils of the Wittenberg school, some closely joined to you by friendship or kinship, some at last also your colleagues in teaching, and then other magnificent and most noble men and distinguished professors, who had long desired your company for the sake of learned conversation, moved by the fame of your name and the deeds you had piously and steadfastly performed, by report and praise of your distinctions and your outstanding services to the commonwealth, and by the monuments of your talent that will last forever. Soon, however, we all also grieved together that your departure, which took you from us only a day after you came, snatched from us the sweetest conversations on many public and private matters, which had barely begun. You are following your illustrious court and, joined at the side like a guardian of mind and body, to the young princes; as their family is most ancient and praised, so we hear that they truly give and show a hope and sure expectation of ancient and distinguished virtue and piety to all, and we pray that God, who alone gives salvation to kings, will with his generous grace wish it to be firm and fixed. We also follow you, whom we have been taken from more quickly than we wished, in spirit, since we cannot in body, with our prayers conceived piously to God for you, and with whatever signs of duty we can give. Therefore, just as the most illustrious princes of Hesse, true and pious nurturers of the Church in this iron age, and our most gracious lords, have embraced you with the kindest affection and humanity in their nation and land, so I have judged that it should be publicly shown to us how welcome and desired you were as a guest at the school. For among other things, when you came early in the morning to the solemn act of our public promotion, with signs of good will, zeal, and special duty, on that very day, shortly after lunch, which the Academy had prepared in your honour, you departed, blessing us; and since our public meeting was to be published by the counsel of the best men, I find no one to whom I would more willingly and gladly dedicate it than to you. For what I seem to hold about the subject in which my speech is engaged, I judge that I owe you something in part, and I must repay with interest what I received from you: you who, in a public disputation held in the year 1571, over which the reverend and distinguished man Caspar Cruciger, Doctor of Theology, presided with great praise, discussed most seriously and learnedly from the very foundation against the [περιτῶν ἐντρωμάτα] Vlachian [Βλαχικά]. Indeed, for a long time the Flacian screech-owls, hissing with their deadly song first against your father-in-law Melanchthon and afterwards against you, and rushing in upon you above all by a certain fate, God punishing men's sins, have desired to nest, as much in the cities and hearts of many as in the Academy on the Elbe, and to hatch their degenerate chicks and bring forth obscene birds, of which the most hideous forms are: Man brutish, bestial, a stump; the corruption of man such as a physical transmutation of substance into another and new one; flesh of another or different species; the conversion and impression of the image of God, and an instantaneous and violent infusion of the grace of the divine Spirit into man, as into empty jugs; man fallen by self-sin [αὐθαμαρτησία], that is, sin itself and the work of the Devil. By these a monstrous theology is introduced (which has no witness in the spiritual experience of the pious in their hearts), and man is stripped of man; physics and theology are mixed, natural things with voluntary ones, and the essence of a thing is confused with its accident [πάθει]. Not to discern these things is ignorance [ἀπαιδευσία], to wrap oneself and others in darkness, not to say anything harsher. I have other reasons, not at all few, for this my [θεσιφω-] mesophonesis, which I now omit, because, lest the letter exceed its measure, I hasten to the end. Such, most distinguished sir, is the true Church: an assembly of the pious, often even of a few, agreeing on true doctrine, and at the same time scattered across regions [κλίματα] very different and separated by a long interval, rightly calling upon God and loving pious fellowship, even though it is not confined, as many think, within the walls of one town or another, or bounded by the limits of a single nation. Finally, it has its defence from God, even though it bears the lordship and the outcries of hypocrites and sycophants, and though the smoke and blasts of Typhons blow against it, who most audaciously invent, spread and propagate dissimilar opinions, and hurl foul abuse at God and men. Therefore, that this my memorial, of whatever kind, and of that union which, as I said at the beginning, has been and is customary among the men of the Academy of Wittenberg, and of that which I have with you in Christ, the head of the Church, and as a testimony of my respect for you, you will kindly accept from me, and I humbly ask that you suffer this my address, perhaps somewhat bold, to be welcome and acceptable to you. I also pray that, if amid your occupations in restoring certain things, useful and necessary doctrines and histories, you can find time to look over these my pages (which, overwhelmed by the multitude of scholastic theological and other mathematical studies, I have not been able to file down to a fine polish), you will not be reluctant to state plainly your judgment and criticism, since I have already been helped and refreshed by your goodwill and delighted by your sincere judgment and candour. I shall therefore rejoice if, from now on too, you will freely and generously show me what you think or approve. I pray with my whole heart to God, the fount of all knowledge and doctrine, that he may kindle the true light and understanding of philosophy and sober theology in many, and confirm it in us more and more; and may he grant that you may long serve, in your course among the most honourable people, in a calmer and more tranquil way, and in those remedies which benefit princes and the life of many men, the Church, and the common studies of learned, pious and sincere doctrine of every kind. Farewell well and happily. Marburg, from our Museum, on the Ides of August, in the year of the Saviour 1588.
Rodolphus Goclenius.
Elenctic Oration.

units.la: EXimia illa & augusta Platonis vox est, Magnifice Domine Rector, Reverendi, & Clarissimi viri, Studiosiq; lectissimi, Philosophiam minimè esse inanem inertemq; contemplationem, sed in beata regnorum gubernatione, addo ego, in Ecclesia Christi, utilem ac fructuosam. Ac prodest omninò discentibus sæpissimè artium usum, cùm in societate humana, tùm verò maximè in doctrina ea, qua salus nostra nititur, ostendere. Quem-admodum enim folia arbori sunt ornamento & usui ad fructus conservandos: Ita congruenter [illegible, ~10 letters] seu Philosophiam velut folia & corticem veritati circumducimus. Illius videlicet sapientiæ cognitionem nobis quoq; tanquam AEgyptiorum illa spolia legitimo furto licet invertere, & ad verū germanumq; usum convertere. Cùm itaque in hoc solenni conventu Academico, antequam primæ laureæ candidati ornentur, omninò, quod instituta majorum volunt, de quopiam argumento mihi verba facienda sint, quantas Dialectica & Physica Ἀκρόασις Aristotelis, quam ἀναλυτικῶς publicé tradidimus, habeat ad primæ sapientiæ sobriam explicationem opportunitates, vel unico exemplo testatius faciam, idq; eo fine, ut ad purioris Philosophiæ, inprimisq; Logicæ & Physicæ studium ac amorem divinarum rerū studiosos, qui certé omnes esse debemus, inflammem atq; exstiexstimulem. Faciam autem id, & quàm possum maximè perspicuè, & observato τῷ μετείφ λόγῳ [?], & ut spero, cum fructu nonnullo. Itaque vobis, optimi adolescentes, dignum officium & mihi honorificum facitis, quod, quam à vobis precibus exposcere de[?]bebam [?], eam vestrapte sponte operam mihi audiendo daturos, silentio vestro, oculorum in nos hilari conjectu, atque aurium liberali erectione, non obscurè præ vobis fertis.
units.tr: This is a fine and noble saying of Plato's, Magnificent Rector, Reverend and Distinguished Sirs, and most select students: philosophy is by no means an empty and idle contemplation, but in the blessed government of kingdoms, I would add, and in the Church of Christ, it is useful and fruitful. Indeed, it is always helpful for learners to show the use of the arts, both in human society and above all in that doctrine on which our salvation rests. For just as leaves are an ornament to a tree and serve to preserve its fruit, so in the same way we wrap philosophy around the truth like leaves and bark. Likewise, we may also turn to our own advantage, by a lawful theft, that knowledge of wisdom, like the spoils of the Egyptians, and convert it to its true and genuine use. Since, then, in this solemn academic assembly, before the first laurels are bestowed on the candidates, I must, as the customs of our ancestors require, speak on some subject, I will show by a single example how far the Dialectic and Physics which we have publicly taught analytically [ἀναλυτικῶς], that is, the Aristotelian lectures, offer opportunities for a sober explanation of first wisdom. I do this so that I may kindle and stir up to the study and love of a purer philosophy, and especially of logic and physics, those who are zealous for divine things, as all of us surely ought to be. I will do this as clearly as I can, observing the [?] method, and, as I hope, with some profit. So, excellent young men, you do me a worthy service and an honour, in that, which I ought to have asked of you in prayer, you of your own accord give me your attention, as your silence, the cheerful turning of your eyes towards us, and the open lifting of your ears make clear.

units.la: PHILOsophia Platonica puriorem quendam hominis statum agnoscit: Agnoscit & illius primigeniæ puritatis corruptionem. Peccati deniq; & labis inseminationem quandam per parentes in liberos agnoscit. Testatur enim in divinum Rationis miraculum ἀναμάρτητον πάθος [?], & hoc ipsum πάθος [?] rationis vim terrena caligine hebetasse & obscurasse, nec tamen penitus extinxisse. Reliquæ enim manserunt scintillæ & igniculi cognitionis Dei, & discriminis boni & mali. Hæc sana est de degenere & corrupta hominis natura Philosophia, & quidem illa sacrarum literarum sententiæ germana: qualis etiam est Hermetis Trismegisti, qui hominis labem & sordes affirmat esse ὕλην, quæ creata opera sequantur, quemadmodum æs rubigo. Congruenter autem hæc dici veritati & sanctæ Scripturæ orthodoxi Theologi fusissimè demonstrarunt. Sed ante annos non ita multos hoc egit FLACIUS, & etiamnum agunt quidam, qui ab ejus sunt disciplina, magno conatu, ut tri[?]sariam doctrinam invehant: Peccatum scilicet à primo ortu inhærens, non esse Naturæ adventitiam contagionem, sed ipsam hominis essentiam & naturam, quanquam corruptam, & ἐνδεχόμενον [?] substantialem, qua ad peccandum rapiamur, quòd elisa, extrita & expulsa imagine Dei, quam causam formalem hominis integri fuisse contendunt, successerit peccatum, ut nova forma & nova imago à Diabolo impressa: Itaq; homo integer & lapsus specie & forma unus homo non sint. Horum θεολογίας [?] etsi solidè confutatas exist imo à nostratibus Theologis; tamen, quia architectus illius dogmatis sese armis mis Philosophicis communit, iisque aliquos minùs instructos Philosophica circumvenit, secumq; in errorum praecipitia abducit, nos clypeo Logico & gladio Physico accincti experiemur, an istius armaturae acies tanta sit, ut veritatem concerpere aut concidere possit.
units.tr: The Platonic philosophy recognises a certain purer state of man. It also recognises the corruption of that original purity. Finally, it recognises a certain inbreeding of sin and stain passed down from parents to children. For it bears witness that the divine wonder of reason suffered a sinless affection [ἀναμάρτητον πάθος], and that this very affection dulled and darkened the power of reason with earthly mist, yet did not wholly extinguish it. For sparks and little fires of the knowledge of God and of the difference between good and evil remained. This philosophy concerning man's degenerate and corrupt nature is sound, and indeed it is in agreement with the true meaning of the sacred letters. Such also is the philosophy of Hermes Trismegistus, who affirms that the stain and filth of man is a matter [ὕλην] which follows the works created, as rust follows bronze. Orthodox theologians have most fully shown that these things agree with the truth and with holy Scripture. But not so many years ago Flacius did this, and some who belong to his school still do it with great effort, in order to bring in this threefold doctrine: that the sin which clings from the first birth is not an accidental contagion of nature, but the very essence and nature of man, though corrupted, and a substantial [?] quality by which we are drawn to sin; for, the image of God, which they maintain was the formal cause of man in his integrity, having been struck out, crushed and driven away, sin has taken its place as a new form and a new image impressed by the Devil. Thus man in his integrity and man fallen are not one man in species and form. Although the theology of these men has been solidly refuted, and indeed by our own theologians, yet because the architect of that dogma arms himself with philosophical weapons, and by these overcomes some who are less instructed in philosophy, and leads them with him into the abysses of error, we, girded with a logical shield and a physical sword, will test whether the edge of this armour is so great that it can tear to pieces or cut down the truth.

units.la: Neq; vero hoc est μελαβαίνειν[?] εἰς ἀλλο[illegible, ~5 letters], seu extra oleas suae professionis vagari. Nam cum & Platonica familia, quod ante attigi, de natura & ἀπαξία hominis differat, ut quae doceat, Philosophiae usum in Dei potissimùm & nostri ipsorum cognitione verti, cumque Peccatum illud Substantiale ex tertio Aristotelis principio, videlicet privatione & corruptione Physica Illyricus exsculpat, ut obtinere possit, Hominis voluntatem in regeneratione & conversione habere se ut truncum & caudicem, esse subiectum impressionis imaginis Dei merè παθητικὸν, adeoq; hostiliter & pertinaciter repugnare gratiae, sicut hoc memini eruditissimè in publica quadam disputatione juventuti Scholasticae ostendere Clarissimum virum Casparum Peucerum, quem honoris causa nomino, cuiq; quantas maximas possum, non tàm meo, quàm totius Academiae nomine, ago gratias, quod hunc conventum & solennem actum sua nobis exoptatissima & honorificentissima praesentia celebriorem reddere dignatus est: Cum, inquam, ex istis fundamentis (at [illegible, ~5 letters] certè) peccatum illud fabricet, φιλοσοφικὴν duntaxat ἀναιρεῖν ad destruendum sum adhibiturus.
units.tr: Nor, indeed, is this to pass over into something else [μεταβαίνειν εἰς ἄλλο], or to wander outside the olive-grounds of one's own profession. For since the Platonic school, as I touched on before, differs about the nature and worth [ἀξία] of man, teaching that the use of philosophy is directed chiefly to the knowledge of God and of ourselves, and since Illyricus carves out that substantial sin from the third principle of Aristotle, namely privation and physical corruption, so that he may maintain that man's will in regeneration and conversion is like a stump and a log, and is the mere passive subject of the impression of God's image, and so stubbornly and hostilely resists grace, as I remember the most learned Caspar Peucer, a most distinguished man, whom I name out of respect, showed very learnedly in a public disputation for the young scholars, and to whom I give the greatest thanks I can, not so much in my own name as in that of the whole Academy, for deigning to make this assembly and solemn act more celebrated by his most desired and most honourable presence: since, I say, from these foundations (but certainly not sound ones) he builds up that sin, I intend to use philosophy alone to destroy it.

units.la: Accedit huc, quòd, templo Delphico inscripta, aurea sententia, & omnium Philosophorum literis tanquam divina celebrata, γνῶθι σεαυτὸν[?] me ad cognitionem naturae hominis, quo haec commentatio & disputatio fere omnis referenda est, & ad refellendum de ea gravissimum, & quidem longè foecundissimū errorem cohortatur. Etenim ut in lerna Hydrae, sicut est in fabulis, prodigiosa foecunditas extitit: sic cùm aliorum, tùm verò hujus erroris uberrima & multiplex est propagatio. Dū enim [illegible, ~8 letters] ingenio suo nimis indulgēs, & hyperbolis abutēs, quasi fugafugacia Dædali simulacra psequitur, ut est in Platonis Menone, vel eò abripitur, ut non vereatur scribere: (cohorresco, me Christe, referens) Carnem Servatoris esse alterius speciei, quàm nostram, & Diabolos tota specie & toto genere differre à Sanctis angelis. Sic usu- venit hoc, quod à Philosopho dictum est: Uno inconvenien- te dato infinita sequuntur. Ac sanè accidit isti, quod iis, qui in luto utrunq; crus impactum habent. Nam quò enixius sese alterutro expedire conantur, eò fortiùs ac profundiùs alterum desigunt. Cum igitur ταφ illius autor, Peccatū illud, quod Originis vo- cant, hoc est, à stirpe generis ac feminis nobis ingeneratum, scri- bit, esse modò hominis naturam, seu essentialem formam & animam rationalem sωθῆς corruptam, modò ipsam voluntatis essentiam, modò ipsum cor inversum & perversum & adulteratam rationem, mi- rum dictu, quantam invehat confusionē Substantiarum & Ac- cidentium, Subjectorū & Adjunctorum, Caussarum & effecto- rum, formarum accidentalium & substantialiū, abstractorum & concretorum, proprie & modificatè dictorum, alterationis deniq; & Interitus, quæ in accurata & τῶς ἀληθείαν apodicticam accómodata ratione docēdi (nam popularium & panegyricarum orationum alia est ratio) probè discernenda sunt. Peccatum ori- ginis essentia aut forma essentialis non est, qualitas & forma ac- cidentaria est. Adjacens & tenacissimè inhærens naturæ malum est, subjectum ipsum non est. Naturæ depravatio est, ipsa natu- ra depravata proprie non est. Non est corruptio naturæ seu sub- stantiæ hominis substantialis, sed alteratio, violatio, vitiatio. Nam primò quicquid uspiā est, aut est ἀνδυνατόςυτον, aut ἐτερυτόςυτον, axioma est, in cujus assertionem conspirarunt quasi omnes veré philosophi, non secus atq; hanc sententiam animo quasi inscul- ptam tuetur omnium gentium non monstrosarum consensio. Quodlibet est aut non est. Et, quod eodem feré recidit, Ens, ali- qui inquiunt, est Substantia vel Qualitas: atq; hæc quidē essen- tialis: ut rationalis; vel accidentalis: ut albus. Jam veró ὑπαρξεῖςυτο· (ut cum autore Epistolæ ad Hebr. loquar) ἁμαρτία non est ἀνυπο- στατῷ & ἀπωλείᾳ π. Nam si peccatum nativum est in hoc rerum genere, corpúsne erit, an spiritus hominis, an facultas essentialis?
units.tr: Moreover, the golden saying inscribed on the temple at Delphi, Know yourself [γνῶθι σεαυτόν], celebrated in the writings of all philosophers as though divine, urges me towards the knowledge of the nature of man, to which almost this whole discussion and dispute must be referred, and towards refuting most serious, and indeed by far most fruitful, error about it. For just as in the fable, in the lernaean Hydra, a prodigious fertility arose, so the spread of this error, as of others, is most abundant and manifold. For while [illegible] he, indulging his own wit too much and abusing hyperboles, pursues, like the fleeing statues of Daedalus, as in Plato's Meno, or is carried so far that he does not hesitate to write (I shudder, Christ, in reporting it): that the flesh of the Saviour is of another kind than ours, and that devils differ from the holy angels in the whole species and the whole genus. So it happens, as the Philosopher said: once one inconvenience is granted, infinite others follow. And indeed it befalls him as it befalls those who have both legs stuck in the mud: the more eagerly they try to free themselves from one, the more firmly and deeply they sink into the other. Therefore, since the author of that doctrine writes that the sin which they call of origin, that is, engendered in us from the stock of the race and the seed, is now the very nature of man, or its essential form and rational soul, corrupted, now the very essence of the will, now the heart itself turned upside down and perverted and reason adulterated, it is a wonder how great a confusion he brings in of substances and accidents, subjects and adjuncts, causes and effects, accidental and substantial forms, abstract and concrete things, things said properly and things said in a modified sense, and finally of alteration and destruction. These must be carefully distinguished in an exact method of teaching which is adapted to the truth and to demonstration (for the method of popular and panegyric speeches is different). Original sin is not the essence or essential form of man; it is an accidental quality and form. It is an evil that clings to and most firmly inheres in nature; it is not the subject itself. It is a depravation of nature; the depraved nature itself is not, properly speaking. It is not a corruption of the substantial nature or substance of man, but an alteration, violation, and vitiation. For first, whatever is either is impossible [ἀνδυνατόςυτον] or is in one way or another [ἐτερυτόςυτον]; this is an axiom, in asserting which almost all truly philosophical men agree, just as the consensus of all non-monstrous nations maintains this sentence as though engraved in the mind. Whatever is, either is or is not. And, which comes almost to the same thing, some say that being is substance or quality: and that substance is either essential, like the rational, or accidental, like the white. Now indeed, as the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews would say, sin is not without subsistence [ὑπαρξις] and destruction. For if native sin is in this class of things, will it be a body, or a spirit of man, or an essential faculty?

units.la: Corpus qui, quæso, fit, cum peccatum in animo fit, corpus autem in animo non fit? Anima enim, cum figuræ & dimensionū expers sit, non potest esse, subjectum capax corporis, certis circumscriptionis terminis definiti. Corpus, credo, qui fit, cum in ipso etiam corpore seu carne & membris inhæreat? Quod si fit spiritus, animus erit ipse, aut specie quiddam differens ab anima, genere autem conveniens. At ipsa animæ ψυχὴ esse nequit, cum ab anima existat corporis vita, informatio & perfectio: peccatū autem hoc corpus non informet, sed deformet, non perficiat hominem, sed inficiat, & interficiat tandem: itaque causa fit vitæ non efficiens, sed deficiens. Et si animi tanquam regia sedes est cor, quod multis Theologis placere video, vel cerebrum, quod medicorum multorum dogma est, quo modo peccatum, quod per omnia viscera diffusum est, & vel minutissimas pervasit particulas lepræ instar, quomodo, inquâ, hæc animi vitiositas sub- stantia esse queat? Si vero in toto esse corpore anima dicatur, quomodo non peccatum edet actiones naturæ singulatum corporis partium consentaneas? hoc est, cor movebit, in ventriculo coquet, in epate recoquet, in venis perficiet, in membra digeret, in corpus mutabit, sufficiet, uniet, instaurabit, redintegrabit. Nec peculiaris in animo spiritus esse potest, cum spiritus naturali ratione non sit in spiritu, at nulla etiam forma est in alia forma. Ec quomodo denique fit δύναμις ψυχικὴ, cum id, propter quod animalis homo non est capax eorum, quæ sunt spiritus Dei, sit naturalis ἀδυναμία, quæ inhabilitatis, ac δύναμις naturalis locum succes- sit. Ac licet dicatur etiam δύναμις κῆξις peccandi ingenita, tamen accidentalis sit, necesse est, cum & sine ea homo possit existere, & sit cum ἀδυναμία & ἀπηξία conjuncta. Et (ut omnia leviter per- stringam) si peccatum est summus animæ rationalis gradus, qui liberi arbitrii appellatione continetur, & ita est [illegible, ~6 letters] π, cur non & in reliquis membris substantia dicitur, cum tota natura hominis fit quasi fermento peccati infecta? Ex his opinor Sole clarius effulgere, peccatum illud & malum in posteros Adami dif-seminatum, non esse in classe substantiarum, & rerum effentia-lium, sed Entium per aliud, ideoq; non minus improprie dici, peccatum esse naturam hominis,quàm fi dicatur, Animam ho-minis esse crafin, vel numerum: Semen esse vim gignentem animal, vulnus esse partem corporis. Genus enim & species debent esse ejusdem categoriae, non petitae ἐξ ἑτέρας συσίας[?], hoc est, è diversa classe & ordine. Unde & hoc liquet, non proprie dici Hominem lapsum peccatum, sed peccatorem, quod & vulgatus Canon docet, Accidentia non συνωνύμως, sed παρωνύμως, & ut loquuntur, voce Concreti subjectis attribui: Et Genus speciei attribui συνωνύμως, non παρωνύμως: ut, Nigror est color, non vero coloratus. Nec quicquam juvat istos, adversus quos disputamus, quod excipiunt, fe non simpliciter dicere, peccatum esse naturam hominis,sed corruptam. Nam hoc dicis, quod ajunt, gratia fit, & popu-lariter, ac ἀκύρως[?] est, imò crassius dicitur. Vulnus proprie non est dilacerata corporis pars,sed laceratio partis. Ruptura, vel ri-ma in speculo aut olla non est difcontinuata vitiataque pars in speculo, aut olla, sed solutio continui, & vitium in speculo, aut olla. Sic peccatum quoq; ingenitum non est effentia hominis corrupta,sed naturæ corruptio, & depravatio in subjecto, quod reliquum est. Ecquis eruditorum est,qui hæc tanquam proprie & apodicticè dicta ferat? Ferrum, quod ignitum est, esse ipsum ignem: Corpus hominis, quod animatum est, esse ipsum animum: Tempus, quod est numerus, seu mefura motus, esse ipsum motum numeratum: Vinum,quod veneno corruptum, hoc est,depravatum est, esse ipsum venenum? Ecquomodo ergo illū proprie loqui putabimus, qui hominem, peccato corruptum, hoc est, infectum, purum putum peccatum esse dicit? Nemo certè doctus eleganter, & æquo animo ferre possit tantam inscitiam Medici, qui, cum febris hectica totum corporis habitum pervasit, ipsum corpus propterea febrim esse dicere ausit? quo modo σεληνιακὸν[?] cum adjuncto confunderetur: aut vesicæ calculum esse morbum ipsum? quo modo id, quod obstruit, cum obstructione ipsa commisceretur, & morbus fieret substantia, qui eruditis medicis qualitas est, & abolito morbo ipse statim calculus abolere-tur, quod non fit: aut deniq; calorem naturale esse febrim ipsam? quod & ipsum secus habet. Destructa enim febri non aboletur calor ipse naturalis, sed reficitur. Quare hic calor nec febris genus, nec pars essentiæ ejus esse potest, sed tantum subjectū est, cui febris accidit. DEinde verū non est, quod Illyricus in definitione peccati στέρησιν[?] de privatione non accidentali, sed substantiali, & corruptionem, hoc est, violationem naturæ hominis, de Physi-ca transmutatione, & corruptione interpretatur. Privatio Aristotelis substantialis est defectus formæ in materia, & hujus inclinatio ad novam formam, quæ in momento introducitur. Ac-cidentalis verò est vacuitas, & absentia accidentis in subjecto. Corruptio Physica generationi opposita, hoc est substātialis, est transmutatio totius compositi substātialis, in aliud novum co-positum substantiale, nullo sensibili remanente. Sed corruptio accidentalis est variatio, facta in subjecto, qua destruitur accidēs. Jam tota, inquit Flacius, natura hominis inversa, & horribiliter transformata est in aliam, vel contrariam naturam: optima essentia rationis in contrariam speciem, seu essentiam: justitia originalis essentialiter conversa est in injustitiam, &c. Sicut angeli boni mutati sunt in aliam speciem, ita ut Diabolus à sancto angelo tota specie differat: vel perinde, ut aurum in plumbum, argetum in scoriam, & vinum in acetum, vel vappam mutatur. Corruptio, inquit, unius, est generatio alterius, ita, ut sicut id, quod corrumpitur, fuit substantia, ita id, quod per eam corruptionem generatur sit nova, & alia substantia. Sed peccatum originale est corruptio naturæ seu substantiæ hominis. Ergo per illam corruptione genita & effecta est alia, & noua hominis substā-tia-
units.tr: What, I ask, is produced when sin is produced in the mind, but body is not produced in the mind? For the soul, since it has no shape or dimensions, cannot be a subject capable of body, which is defined by fixed limits of circumscription. What body, I suppose, is produced when sin clings to the body itself, that is, to the flesh and limbs? But if it is a spirit, then it will be the mind itself, or something differing from the soul in species but agreeing with it in genus. Yet it cannot be the soul's life [ψυχή] itself, since the life of the body comes from the soul as its form and perfection. Sin does not inform the body but deforms it; it does not perfect the man but infects him and at last kills him. So it becomes a cause of life not efficient but deficient. And if the heart is the royal seat of the mind, as I see pleases many theologians, or the brain, as is the doctrine of many physicians, how can this vice of the mind be a substance, when sin is diffused through all the viscera and has penetrated even the smallest particles like leprosy? But if the soul is said to be in the whole body, how would sin not produce actions of nature consistent with each part of the body? That is, it would move the heart, cook in the stomach, recook in the liver, perfect in the veins, digest into the limbs, change into the body, supply, unite, restore and make whole again. Nor can there be a peculiar spirit in the mind, since by natural reason spirit is not in spirit, and no form is in another form. And how finally does it become a psychic power [δύναμις ψυχικὴ], since that on account of which the natural man is not capable of the things of the Spirit of God is a natural inability [ἀδυναμία], which takes the place of incapacity and natural power? And although it is said to be an inborn habit of sinning [δύναμις κῆξις], it must still be accidental, since man can exist without it, and it is joined with inability and unfitness [ἀπηξία]. And (to touch on everything lightly) if sin is the highest degree of the rational soul, which is contained under the name of free will, and so it is [illegible], why is it not also said to be a substance in the remaining members, since the whole nature of man has become, as it were, leavened with the poison of sin? From these things, I think, it shines clearer than the sun that the sin and evil spread to the posterity of Adam is not in the class of substances and essential things, but among beings through something else. Therefore it is no less improper to say that sin is the nature of man than to say that the soul of man is a crasis or a number, that semen is the power generating an animal, or that a wound is a part of the body. For genus and species must belong to the same category, not be drawn from another substance [ἐξ ἑτέρας οὐσίας], that is, from a different class and order. Whence this also is clear: man fallen is not properly called sin but sinner, as the common canon teaches: accidents are attributed to subjects not synonymously [συνωνύμως] but paronymously [παρωνύμως], and, as they say, by the word of the concrete; whereas a genus is attributed to its species synonymously, not paronymously, as black is a colour but not coloured. Nor does it help those with whom we dispute that they except and say they do not simply call sin the nature of man, but corrupted nature. For this, as they say, is said by grace and in a popular way, and is inexact [ἀκύρως]; indeed it is said more crudely. A wound is properly not a torn part of the body but the laceration of a part. A rupture or crack in a mirror or pot is not a discontinuous and vitiated part of the mirror or pot, but a breach of continuity and a defect in the mirror or pot. So inborn sin is not the corrupted essence of man, but a corruption and depravation of nature in the subject that remains. Which of the learned would accept these things as said properly and apodictically? Iron that is red-hot is itself fire; the body of man that is animated is itself the mind; time, which is number or measure of motion, is itself the motion numbered; wine corrupted by poison, that is, depraved, is itself poison. How then shall we think he speaks properly who says that man corrupted by sin, that is, infected, is pure sin? No learned man could calmly and elegantly bear such ignorance in a physician who dared to call the body itself a fever because hectic fever has pervaded the whole habit of the body; or that the bladder stone is the disease itself, how the lunar [σεληνιακὸν] thing would be confused with its adjunct; or, finally, that natural heat is the fever itself, which is otherwise too. For when the fever is destroyed, the natural heat itself is not abolished but restored. Wherefore this heat can be neither a genus of fever nor a part of its essence, but only the subject to which the fever happens. Next, it is not true that Illyricus, in defining sin, interprets the privation as substantial rather than accidental, and the corruption, that is the violation, of the nature of man as a physical transmutation and corruption. The privation of Aristotle is a substantial defect of form in matter, and the inclination of this matter toward a new form, which is introduced in an instant. Accidental privation, however, is the emptiness and absence of an accident in a subject. Physical corruption, opposed to generation, that is, substantial corruption, is the transmutation of a whole substantial compound into another new substantial compound, with nothing sensible remaining. But accidental corruption is a variation made in a subject, by which the accident is destroyed. Now the whole, says Flacius, nature of man has been turned upside down and horribly transformed into another or contrary nature: the best essence of reason into a contrary species or essence: original justice has been essentially converted into injustice, etc. Just as good angels have been changed into another species, so that the devil differs from the holy angel in the whole species; or just as gold is changed into lead, silver into dross, and wine into vinegar or flat wine. The corruption of one thing, he says, is the generation of another, so that just as that which is corrupted was a substance, so that which is generated by that corruption is a new and different substance. But original sin is the corruption of the nature or substance of man. Therefore through that corruption a different and new substance of man has been begotten and made.

units.la: Hæc ergo qualia sint videamus. Cum ex non corpore fit corpus, ex non cane canis, privatio illa, quę motus est causa sine qua non, substantialis est: Accidentalis vero, cum ex immusico musicum, ex impolito politum fieri dicimus. Cum ex homine fit non homo, ut elementū aliquod vel serpens, hæc φθορὰ seu corruptio φθαρτικὴ est. Cum vero ex nigro albus, ex justo injustus, hæc corruptio accidentalis est. Id quod fateri cogũtur, vel quibus est semiuncia veri, ut ait Poeta. Si igitur peccatum [illegible, ~8 letters] est privatio, vel corruptio substantialis, quæro, cur habere illud definiatur: Ex justo non justum factum esse, & non potius ex homine non hominem factum esse? Et si omninò ita substantia nostra optima evasit pessima, ut si aurum purissimum in plumbum, vitis in labruscam, olea in oleastrum conversa sint (hi enim, ut antè attigi, sunt Illyrici, & suorum flosculi, hæc pigmenta, imò veriusobjectæ nebulæ, quibus à vero judicio simpliciores abducuntur) si, inquam, ejusmodi essentialis transmutatio hominis à peccato extitit, qui homines amplius vocabimur, cum sublata pristina forma, & succedente nova, tollatur rei nomen & definitio? ut cùm ex & in caseo, pereunte hujus forma, nascitur vermis, non dicitur amplius caseus, sed vermis. [illegible, ~20 letters], id est, æquũ est à formis rebus nomina imponi. Præterea si fit in renatis mutatio substantialis injustitiæ in vere perfectéque contrariam substantialem justitiam, hoc profectò etiam dogmatistes cum suis fateri ex natura contrariorum cogetur: Sicut peccatum fuit perfecta imago Diaboli in impiis, ita justitiam eorum, postquam renati sunt, esse perfectam imaginem Dei, & ex consequenti nullas hærere peccati reliquias in sanctis, & conversis, nisi forte in inferioribus duntaxat viribus, justitiamq; non consistere in imputatione alienæ justitiæ, sed in formali justitia, & inhærente, qui omnes sunt salsissimi, & ab Ecclesia rejecti errores. Ac ut arctius eos Aristotelea Philosophia, ex qua arma contra veritatem sumserunt, premamus, & deductione ad incomincommodum urgeamus. Si natura seu substantia transforma-ta est in contrariam, peccatum, peccatum sane ut generabile se habebit. Substantiae enim seu naturae est generatio. Si ut generabile, quomodo non erit corruptibile? Si corruptibile, quomodo non aliud generabit? Generabit ergo aut aliud peccatum, idq; homine jam ad corruptionem tendente, quod est ἀδύνατος[?], quia mors est tanquam via, & causa sine qua non restituendae integritatis: Aut justitiam procreabit, quod si absurdum non est, quid tum, cum causa non sit toto genere deterior suo effecto, & simile procreet simile? Ecquis satis sobrius credat, ipsam animam rationalem fuisse justitiam originalem, eandemq; essentialiter permu-tatam esse in injustitiam, ac in renatis vicissim permutari & trans-formari in justitiam. Non enim injustitia unquam mutatur in ju-stitiam, ut nunquam nigror transit in alborem, sed injustum po-test fieri justum, ut ex nigro album. Quia homo tanquam subje-ctum utriusq; contrarii vicissim capax est. Recte dicimus, Frigi-dum esse facta calidum, non autem frigus factum esse calorem, aut privationem frigoris esse ipsam ἐναντίον[?] caloris. Ita probe etiam dicimus, justam & puram naturam factam esse injustam, & im-puram, non vero puritatem esse factam impuritatem. Quid? quod, si stabit ille πλασματίας λόγος, conficietur ex eo, Animam & ὑποκείμενον seu subjectum esse, & συμβεβηκός, seu accidens simul, ipsamque in se recipere contraria, & simul esse ipsa contraria, quo quid monstrosius fingi possit, non video. Quod enim fuit, qui diceret, cum nulla absurditate conjunctum esse, statuere peccatum ἔμφυτον esse & accidens & substantiam, quandoquidem & accidentia & substantia hominis simul sunt depravata, hoc ergo tam puerile est, ut refutationis me suppudeat. Qualis enim haec est consecutio: In lepra & homini adjunctus color & ipsa substan-tia inficitur. Ergo lepra est accidens & substantia simul? Haec omnia tam manifesta sunt, ut negari non possint, nisi ab eo, quem Orestes ipse insanus juret non sanum esse hominem. Itaq; ne de rationis statu videantur omnino deturbati, aliquid largiuntur, Substantiam scilicet hominus manere in partibus ignobilioribus dun-taxat, in praestantissima vero parte interiisse, seu optimam formam animae in pessimam essentialiter esse transformatam, partem autem optimam volunt esse liberum arbitrium, idemque volunt postea etiam esse pessimam partem, seu formam. Id vero ἀδύνατον est, subsistantiae uni & individuae, qualis homo est, detrahi partem optimam, & subsistentiam tamen permanere: quae tanquam in puncto ἀτόμῳ posita est, vel sese habet ut figura vel numerus aliquis definitus, cui nihil addi potest, aut adimi tam exiguum, quin tota ejus essentia perierit. Abolito ergo libero illo arbitrio, fieri nullo modo potest, ut adhuc superstes sit eadem hominis substantia. At non dicimus, inquiunt, Cor vel liberum arbitrium (mire enim variant suis nomenclaturis) simpliciter exolescere, aut aboleri, sed essentialiter transmutari: sicut propter lapsum Adae totus mundus non est abolitus, sed essentialiter mutatus. Sed contra nemo unquam essentialem transmutationem pro alia re intellexit, nec intelligere poterit, quam pro tali corruptione, qua tendit res ad non esse, & ad quam sequitur novae rei procreatio. Non esse autem regenerationem hominis intelligendam de Physica παλιγγενεσία, Christus luculenter ostendit, cum de tali imaginatione Nicodemum castiget. Cumq; coeli & coelestium corporum neq; materia, neq; forma, neq; naturalis qualitas corrupta fit, substantialiter totum mundum esse mutatum, nemo concesserit, nisi qui cum ratione insaniat. Sed adhibent ad id, quod volunt, comparationem a ruina domus pulcerrimae & formae eius interitu. Reliqua, inquiunt, sunt de homine primaevo, seu priscino, velut destructa domo ruinosa quaedam rudera. O ruinosae & perditae potius causae, miseram substructionem & ruinosum fulcrum. Domus enim, quatenus domus, non denotat substantiam, nec a natura ita dicitur, sed a forma artificiosa, ac cum vitio quodam destruitur domus ita, ut materies aliqua reliqua sit, fit ξύμπαλιν copositi artificiosa dissolvidissolutio. At homini labes peccati, non concreata quidem,sed concreta adjacet,salva,per omnē vitam,corporis & animæ conjunctione,salvis facultatib. essentialibus, ut δυνάμει[?] illa χρηστὴ[?], sub quam cadit τὸ γνωστὸν[?] ἐκ Θεοῦ[?], de quo Paulus c.1. ad Rom. Definitionem etiam accidentis Porphyrianam in patrocinium suæ causæ advocant. Accidens est, quicquid adest, vel abest, præter subjecti corruptionem. Jam si peccatum, inde usq; a primo ortu contractum, non potest abesse, citra subjecti interitum, eo quod homo vetus mortificatur in separatione peccati, statuedum putant, peccatum illud non esse qualitatem accidentariam. Ἄτοπα τινὰ[?], ἢ ἐν αὐτοῖς σύμφωνα[?]. Hæc tùm ab-surdè dicuntur, tùm secum ipsa vehementer pugnant. Primùm, peccatum originis separari posse concedunt à subjecto, & tamen asserunt esse optimam subjecti substantiam, cùm fieri omninó non possit, ut aliquid sit in subjecto, & simul subjectum ipsum. Deinde mortificatio hominis veteris nequaquam est subjecti interitus(ut nec subjecti corruptio erat,quādo originale justitiam homo amisit.Quod si dicant peccatum istud non separari naturaliter,sed vi divinæ omnipotetiæ, quæ nos exutos mortali corpore tandem resuscitatura sit justos & expertes omnis labis,id libenter dabimus: Sed nihilominus interim peccatum separabile est aliquid ratione,& substantia hominis erit eadem,in vita illa beata & sanctissima,quæ fuit in hac ærumnosa,& sordidata. Debebant igitur isti distinguere in accidetis illa descriptione, inter corruptionem Physicam,& Logicam,inter actū, & potentiam. Peccatum originis etsi totum ante mortem naturæ exui, seu citta compositi dissolutionem abesse ab eo non possit,in præsente hominis statu: abest tamen ab eo præter subjecti corruptionem logicam: mens enim nostra logica ἀφαιρέσει[?] abstrahit peccatū ab anima,ut nigredinem à corvo,& albedinem à cygno. Etsi enim reipsa nigror corvo detrahi nequeat: potest tamen mutato colore corvus albus intelligi, sine interitu corvi,in quo est:quia ni-grror non inest τῷ αὐτῷ[?] corvo,nec pertinet ad ejus essentiam.
units.tr: Let us see, then, what kind of change this is. When body comes from non-body, or dog from non-dog, that privation, which is the cause without which the motion does not happen, is substantial. Accidental change is when we say that something becomes musical from unmusical, or polished from unpolished. When man becomes non-man, as when he becomes some element or a serpent, this is corruption [φθορὰ], the destructive kind of corruption. When white comes from black, or unjust from just, the corruption is accidental. Those who are forced to admit this are the ones who have "a half-truth," as the poet says. So if sin is a privation or substantial corruption [illegible], I ask why it is defined as: that the just man has become unjust, and not rather that the man has become not-man? And if our substance has turned out so completely worst from best, as if the purest gold had been changed into lead, the vine into wild grape, or the olive into the wild olive (for these are the Illyrians and their little flowers, these paints, or rather the clouds thrown up to draw simpler people away from true judgement), if, I say, such an essential transformation of man has come about through sin, why should we still call them men, since when the former form is removed and a new one takes its place, the name and definition of the thing are also removed? Just as when cheese, once its form has perished, becomes a worm, it is no longer called cheese but worm. [illegible], that is, it is right that names are given to things according to their forms. Furthermore, if in the regenerate there is a substantial change from substantial injustice into a substantial justice that is truly and perfectly contrary, then the dogmatists with their party will surely be forced to admit this from the nature of contraries: just as sin was the perfect image of the devil in the wicked, so their justice, after they are reborn, is the perfect image of God, and consequently there remain no remnants of sin in the saints and converted, unless perhaps in the lower powers only; and that justice does not consist in the imputation of another's righteousness, but in a formal and inherent righteousness. These are all most foolish errors, rejected by the Church. And so that we may press them more tightly with the Aristotelian philosophy, from which they took up arms against the truth, and urge them with the argument from absurdity: if nature or substance has been transformed into its contrary, then sin will behave as something capable of being generated. For generation belongs to substance or nature. If it is capable of generation, how is it not capable of corruption? If capable of corruption, how will it not generate something else? It will therefore generate either another sin, when the man is already tending towards corruption, which is impossible [ἀδύνατον], because death is as it were the way and the cause without which the integrity cannot be restored; or else it will produce justice. And if this is not absurd, what then? Since a cause is not in every respect worse than its effect, and like produces like. Who who was even moderately sober would believe that the rational soul itself was original justice, and that this same thing was essentially changed into injustice, and that in the regenerate it is in turn changed and transformed into justice. For injustice is never changed into justice, just as blackness never passes into whiteness; but what is unjust can become just, as black can become white. This is because man, as subject, is capable in turn of either contrary. We rightly say that the cold has become warm, but not that cold has become heat, or that the privation of cold is itself the contrary [ἐναντίον] of heat. So too we properly say that a just and pure nature has become unjust and impure, but not that purity has become impurity. What then? If that fabricated argument [πλασματίας λόγος] stands, it will follow that the soul is both a subject [ὑποκείμενον] and an accident [συμβεβηκός] at the same time, and that it receives contraries in itself and is at the same time the contraries themselves. I do not see what more monstrous thing could be invented. For it was someone who said, as though without any absurdity, that sin is innate and is both an accident and a substance, since both the accidents and the substance of man have been corrupted at the same time. This is so childish that I am ashamed to refute it. For what kind of inference is this? In leprosy the colour adhering to a man and the very substance are infected. Therefore leprosy is an accident and a substance at the same time? All these things are so plain that they cannot be denied, except by one whom Orestes himself, in his madness, would swear is not a sane man. And so, lest they seem wholly to have been thrown off from the state of reason, they concede something: that the substance of man remains only in the baser parts, but in the most excellent part it has perished; or that the best form of the soul has been essentially transformed into the worst; and they want the best part to be free choice, and the same they want afterwards to be the worst part or form. But this is impossible [ἀδύνατον]: for from one and indivisible substance, such as man is, the best part cannot be taken away while the substance nevertheless remains. Such a substance is set as if at an indivisible point, or stands like a figure or some definite number, to which nothing can be added or taken away, however small, without its whole essence perishing. Therefore, once that free choice is abolished, it is in no way possible that the same substance of man should still survive. But, they say, we do not claim that the heart or free choice (for they vary wonderfully in their terminology) simply fades away or is abolished, but is essentially changed, just as through the fall of Adam the whole world was not abolished, but essentially changed. But on the contrary, no one has ever understood an essential transformation to mean something other than a corruption by which a thing tends towards non-being, and after which the production of a new thing follows; nor will anyone be able to understand it otherwise. That the regeneration of man is not to be understood as physical palingenesia [παλιγγενεσία], Christ shows plainly when he rebukes Nicodemus for such an imagining. And since neither the matter, nor the form, nor the natural quality of the heavens and the heavenly bodies is corrupted, no one would concede that the whole world has been substantially changed, except one who is raving with reason. But they bring in, for what they want, a comparison from the ruin of a most beautiful house and its destruction. The rest, they say, are certain rubbish of the ruined house, concerning the first or primitive man. O ruinous and rather lost cause, miserable foundation and ruinous support! For a house, as a house, does not denote a substance, nor is it so called by nature, but by artifice of form; and when a house is destroyed through some defect, so that some material remains, the artificial composite is dissolved in reverse. But to man the stain of sin, not indeed created with him but grown into him, clings, while the union of body and soul remains intact throughout life, and the essential faculties remain intact, such as that good power under which falls the knowable of God [τὸ γνωστὸν ἐκ Θεοῦ], of which Paul speaks, Rom. 1. They also summon in defence of their cause the Porphyrian definition of accident: An accident is whatever is present or absent without the corruption of the subject. If, then, sin, contracted from the first origin, cannot be absent without the destruction of the subject, since the old man is mortified in the separation of sin, they think that sin must be judged not to be an accidental quality. Absurd things, or things consistent in themselves [Ἄτοπα τινά, ἢ ἐν αὐτοῖς σύμφωνα]. These things are both absurdly said and violently at odds with themselves. First, they concede that original sin can be separated from the subject, and yet they assert that it is the best substance of the subject, although it is entirely impossible for something to be in a subject and at the same time be the subject itself. Next, the mortification of the old man is by no means the destruction of the subject, just as it was not the corruption of the subject when man lost original justice. But if they say that this sin is not separated naturally, but by the power of divine omnipotence, which will at last raise us, stripped of mortal body, just and free of all stain, we will gladly grant that; but nevertheless sin is in the meantime separable in reason, and the substance of man will be the same in that blessed and most holy life as it was in this wretched and defiled one. They ought therefore to have distinguished, in that description of an accident, between physical and logical corruption, between act and potency. Original sin, although in the present state of man it cannot be wholly stripped off before death, or be absent from him apart from the dissolution of the composite, is nevertheless absent from him apart from the logical corruption of the subject. For our logical mind, by abstraction, separates sin from the soul, as blackness from the raven and whiteness from the swan. For although blackness cannot really be stripped from the raven, the raven can nevertheless be conceived as white, with its colour changed, without the raven in which it is perishing; because blackness does not inhere in the same raven and does not belong to its essence.

units.la: Et quidem hæc, quæ de separatione mentis dico, adeò vera sunt, ut etiam id quod καθ' αὐτὸ est, & proprium rei, separetur quodam modo ἐπινοίᾳ[?] & vi intellectus à subjecto. Cùm enim in accuratissima definitione non adhibeantur propria, definiens separat proprium à subjecto: ut hominem definiens abstrahit eum à facultate ridendi, hoc est, quatenus eum definit è materia & forma, considerat eum, non habita ratione aptitudinis ad ridendum: quantò magis accidens commune, quod non est καθ' αὐτὸ, secernetur à subjecto, ut intellectus in eo ponere possit accidens contrarium: verbi gratia, in cygno atrorem. Eadem ratione homini vi animi fictrice attribuere possum pro peccato justitiam, & contrà, salvis nihilominus hominis partibus essentialibus & integrantibus omnibus. Neq; verò peccatum separatum & divulsum à natura statuimus, perinde ac si in ea non inhære-ret fixissimis radicibus, aut esset abstractum, & idea aliqua, extra substantiam, seu naturam humanam: sed mentis illa abstractione distinguimus subjectam naturam, ab adjacente naturæ vitio, ne opus Dei cum non opere Dei cōfundamus: ac ut longè aliud est, distinguere duas naturas in Christo, quàm divellere, discerpere, & separare eas reipsa à se invicem: Sic & longè aliud est, inter naturam, & concretam naturæ labem discernere: & hanc ab illa reipsa penitus secernere, ac auferre: quemadmodum excrementa in corpore animalis ab utili humore segregantur.
units.tr: Indeed, what I say about the separation of the mind is so true that even what is per se and proper to a thing is separated in some way, by thought and the power of the intellect, from its subject. In the most exact definition proper attributes are not used, so the definer separates the proper attribute from the subject. When defining man, for instance, one abstracts him from the faculty of laughing: insofar as one defines him from matter and form, one considers him without regard to his aptitude for laughing. How much more, then, can a common accident, which is not per se, be set apart from the subject, so that the intellect can posit a contrary accident in it, for example blackness in a swan. By the same reasoning I can, by the creative power of the mind, attribute righteousness in place of sin to a man, and the reverse, while the man's essential and integral parts all remain. Nor do we claim that sin is torn away and separated from nature, as if it did not cling to nature with the firmest roots, or were an abstracted idea outside the substance or human nature. Rather, by that mental abstraction we distinguish the underlying nature from the vice that adheres to it, lest we confuse the work of God with what is not the work of God. Just as it is far different to distinguish two natures in Christ from tearing and rending them and really separating them from one another, so it is far different to discern between nature and its concrete corruption, and to separate and remove the one entirely from the other in reality, just as excrements are segregated from useful humour in the body of an animal.

units.la: Postremò ne hoc quidem negari potest, in hac etiam vita peccatum aliqua ex parte esse χωριστὸν[?], & separari à corde, per regenerationem: quò fit, ut David petat à Deo creationem novi cordis, hoc est, renovationem, ipsa Scriptura interprete.
units.tr: Finally, it cannot be denied that even in this life sin is in some respect separable [χωριστόν] and is separated from the heart through regeneration. Hence David, with Scripture itself as interpreter, asks God for the creation of a new heart, that is, for renewal.

units.la: Ajunt porrò, peccatum ἔμφυτον[?] esse maximè ἐνεργητικόν[?], & in perpetuo motu. Actiones autem tribui substantiis. Quid audio? Ergo dolor nihil agis, ergo morbus nihil agit, calor & frigus nihil agunt. Actiones & perpessiones sunt substantiarum: quis neget? Sed annon illæ ipsæ substantiæ per qualitates sunt efficaces? Omninò. Accidentia dant formæ, ut sic agat, ait Scaliger. Ideo autem tribuuntur ἐνέργειαι[?] substantiis, quia nullum accidens agit nisi per vim suæ substantiæ, ut iterum cum Scaligero loquar. Sed ad ravim etiam inculcant, Deum non irasci mero accidenti, quod propinquum est non enti (Arist. 6. Philos.): Accidens non posse sustinere reatum, & Scripturam in describen-do peccato uti substantialibus verbis. Atque hinc inferunt, peccatum esse hominis naturam ipsam. Hic veré respondemus: Fie-ri non posse, ut accidens subsistat sine subjecto, seu, ut Philoso-phus inquit, Accidentis essentiam esse ἐνυπάρχειν[?]: id est, inhære-re. Accusat ergo Deus & ream peragit ipsam Substantiam, & non solùm accidens malum, quod hoc absq; subjecto substan-tiali esse nequeat. Quomodo medicus curat corpus ipsum, non autem morbum solùm qui in corpore, utpote subjecto, inhæret, Merito igitur nativa vitiositas cum ipso subjecto seu toto homine accusatur & damnatur, ut merito magistratus punit & fur-tum, & furem, nec tamen furtum, sed furem laqueo suspendit. Ἀπολογία[?] igitur committitur, & ita purum putum sophisma deprehenditur. Substantialibus verbis nominatur, & arguitur peccatum. Ergo est substantia. Imò verò subjectum peccati ne-cessario simul est comprehendendum, cum fine eo contrario-rum mutatio nunquam fieri possit, alterius in alterum, ut do-cent omnes Physicorum familiæ.
units.tr: They further say that sin is innate [ἔμφυτον] and especially active [ἐνεργητικόν], and in perpetual motion. Actions, however, are attributed to substances. What do I hear? Then pain does nothing, disease does nothing, heat and cold do nothing. That actions and passions belong to substances: who would deny it? But are not those very substances effective through their qualities? Certainly. "Accidents give the form so that it acts," says Scaliger. Activities [ἐνέργειαι] are attributed to substances because no accident acts except through the power of its substance, as I again say with Scaliger. But they also press the point that God is not angry at a mere accident, which is close to non-being (Aristotle, Metaphysics 6); that an accident cannot bear guilt; and that Scripture, in describing sin, uses substantial words. From this they infer that sin is the very nature of man. Here we reply truly: an accident cannot subsist without a subject, or, as the Philosopher says, the essence of an accident is to inhere [ἐνυπάρχειν], that is, to be in something. God therefore accuses and condemns the substance itself, and not only the evil accident, since this cannot exist without a substantial subject. Just as a physician cures the body itself, and not merely the disease which inheres in the body as in its subject, so the innate vitiosity is rightly accused and condemned together with the subject itself, or the whole man. So too a magistrate rightly punishes theft and the thief, yet hangs the thief on the gallows, not the theft. A plea [ἀπολογία] is therefore being made, and so a plain and simple sophism is detected. Sin is named and charged in substantial words. Therefore it is a substance. Indeed, rather, the subject of sin must necessarily be comprehended together with it, since change from one contrary into the other can never occur without the subject, as all the schools of the natural philosophers teach.

units.la: Præterea quòd Scriptura vocabulis, quæ ἰδίως[?] substantiæ notationes sunt, de peccato utitur, nihil mirum est, cùm nomi-na substantiarum & subjectorum sæpè pro adjunctis, hoc est, pro qualitatibus in subjectis inhærentibus, & pro actionibus qualitatum ponantur, per auxesin seu emphaticam metonymiam, quo modo etiam peccatum ipsum pro re extremè vitiosa, & maledictioni subjecta, & caro pro carnali affectione accipitur.
units.tr: Moreover, that Scripture uses of sin words which properly denote substances is no cause for wonder, since the names of substances and subjects are often put for their adjuncts, that is, for the qualities inhering in subjects, and for the actions of qualities, by way of auxesis or emphatic metonymy. In this way sin itself is also taken for a thing extremely wicked and liable to curse, and flesh for carnal affection.

units.la: Sic porrò ratiocinantur: Homo est peccator. Peccatoris forma est peccatum. Ergo homo est peccatum: Et ex conse-quenti, quenti peccatū est forma hominis. Sed (malum) in qua Schola ita argumentari didicerunt. Stultitiæne an Sapientiæ. Homines isti sunt stulti. Stulti forma est stultitia. Ergo homines isti sunt mera stultitia? Respondeto pro me Echo. Quid fit ex malè confutis? Utis, hoc est, nullus Syllogismus. At verò, inquit, bene infertur istud ex regula quæ traditur in doctrina Arist. quæ categorias antecedit. Cum alterū de altero tanquā de subjecto dicitur, quicquid de prædicato dicitur, id omne de subjecto quoq; dicetur. Minimè vero.
