Regula hæc manet vera, sed exemplum non cōgruit ad eam: ut Solis motus legitimus est in cœlo perpetuò, ubi tanquā horologium est minimè fallax, etsi stolidus ædituus templi horologium non rectè dirigat ad cursum Solis. Sed cur exemplum non quadrat ad canonem? Quod laboret vitio malæ subsumtionis seu Elenchi ἐλεγχος ὁρων[?], id est, expositionis terminorum: itaque deprehendas hic tanquam scopas dissolutas. Quis enim est tam plumbeus in Logicis, qui non intelligat esse quatuor terminos, Homo, Peccator, Peccatoris forma, Peccatum? Plurimùm autem anhelant & sudant, ut se expediant, ne videantur confiteri Diabolum conditorem esse & principiū substantiarum malarum, sed frustra. Positis enim principiis istis, quibus utuntur, scopulus Manichæi dogmatis evitari non potest. Ac hic maximè evenit eis, quod illis, qui in cœno hærent, qui dum pedem alterum, quo sese expediant, tollere nituntur, altius figunt alterum. Affirmant eandem substantiam posse habere duos diversissimos auctores, alterum verum conditorem Deum, alterum destructorem Diabolum, & tamen rem esse numero unam. Hujus autem rei tale proponunt exemplum: Arbor bona, cum mutatur in malam, nō duæ sunt arbores, sed una: causa autem alia est bonæ, alia malæ arboris. Sic illi quidem: sed quid hoc eos juverit? Num maliria[?], quæ arbor mala est, est arbos ipsa, sicut peccatum dicunt esse [?] animam malam. Arbor mala nō simpliciter significat arborem, sed arborem cum qualitate litate' inhærente, quæ mutabilis est. Et dum ex bona arbore fit mala,eadem arbor est subjectum utriusq; qualitatis,& mutatio aut destructio ista non efficit novam substantiam arboris, sed variationem seu alterationem. Nec habet duos auctores arbor, unum à quo procreetur bona,alterum à quo procreetur mala. Si per destructore intelligerent causam alterationis cujusdam,cōcedi posset. Nō enim causa alterans est causa generans aut creans,ut interpolator est renovator vestis,non procreator. Causa calefaciens aquam, ut ignis, non est auctor ipsius substantiæ aquæ,cùm in alteratione subjectū manet idē,eiq; tantùm qualitas nova indatur. Quomodo ergo destructor talis alterans, dicetur auctor substantiæ ipsius ? Sed destructorem pro conditore intelligunt,cùm dicant hominem non renatum esse opus Diaboli,& imaginem Satanæ, nec velint in homine factam destructionem esse accidens quoddam:cum denique huc transferant illud Aristotelis:Interitus unius,est alterius ortus. Tandem,qui, inquiunt, Dæmon non possit esse effectrix causa substantiæ,cum sint innumerae res, quæ substantias ex aliis substantiis faciunt? Cocus enim in olla carnem coquens ex aqua facit aërem. Et rustica interventu motus ex lacte potest conficere butyrum, & vinitor ex aqua & uvæ flocibus facit loram. Quid ni ergo Diabolus πολυτεχνώταλ[?] invertere possit hominis substantiam,& diversam à priori producere?Sed propterea quod isti oculis utuntur(ut est apud Plautum)oculis item nostris dent aliquid,æquum est.Cer-tissimus[?] enim abiitis[?] committi fallaciam à non causa tanquam causa. Quod ex aqua fit aër seu vapor, dum coquitur ad ignem, non certè id hominis opus est,sed naturæ:ignis siquidem est,qui partes aquæ omnes penetrat, segregat, attenuat, rarefacit, & in vaporem digerit,cùm homo tantùm applicet,& conjungat ista agentia naturalia, sitq; ejus actionis administer. Sic natura est, quæ facit loram,opera hominis tantùm ministrante,& miscente aquam & succum purgamentorum uvæ, ut hæc duo fiant unum: uvam : Sic medicus curans [illegible, ~5 letters] non facit carnem in corpore humano, sed natura reliqua, quæ instauratur, & per ipsa medicamenta, quæ res naturales sunt, ipsum nutrimentum. Sic quando mammosa Nisa ex lacte conficit caseos, dato, quòd caseus sit nova substantia, cùm revera sit opus alterationis, non generationis, ut corpora imperfectè concreta, seu meteora pleraque, sed posito illo, opus tamen istud non est mammosæ Nisæ, aut lacertosæ Phyllidos, sed naturæ. In lacte siquidem est natura & internum principium, ut ex eo possit fieri caseus. Homo tantùm addit instrumenta, ut baculum, quibus perficiatur segregatio partium pinguium & tenuium, quibusq; fiat coagulatio, exsiccatio, induratio. Sic homo nō est [illegible, ~6 letters] hujus compositi, quod Sal dicitur, sed natura ope artificii ex aqua salsa educit salè, qui [illegible, ~4 letters] inest in aqua illa. Sic quod de [illegible, ~9 letters] & [illegible, ~9 letters] dicunt chymici & æruscatores, per lapidem illum admirabilem, quem vocant Philosophicum, rectè & accuratè præparatum, omnia metalla converti posse in aurum, & inferiora, id est, præter aurum cætera metalla transmutari posse in argentum. Ad id verè respondetur, in lapide illo rubro, quo aurum, & candido, quo argentum fieri dicitur, non esse vim verè convertendi metalla, cum non habeat vim tingendi alia ratione, quàm si fiat crama, & aurum factitium nihil aliud sit quàm massa mixta, seu crama metallicum (idem de argento factitio judicium esto) ut verè judicat Claudius Triuncurianus[?]. Fatemur, inquit, lapidum isto-rum accuratissimè præparatorum partes [illegible, ~12 letters] nutissimis quibusq; partibus ejus metalli fusi, in quod injiciuntur, ut fiat quasi crama quoddam metallicum. Etenim si metallum nihil aliud est quàm aqua terrea, multo frigore congelata, quæ propterea nō nisi multo calore restitui potest in pristinum fluorem: non est mirum, aurum & argentum posse fieri unum per crasin, præsertim cùm pulvis auri accuratissimè præparatus in argentum fusum projicitur. Ergo fit UNUM per CRASIN, non autem unum per generationem. Proinde forma auri remanet in materia & partibus auri, ut & forma argenti remanet in materia argenti, non secus atq; in cramate, ut in vino aqua diluto, seu mixto cum aqua, remanet utriusq; nempe vini & a-quae forma. Ut igitur homini & arti, qui est habitus in homine, sic & Diabolo ἀλλοιωτ[?] est Metamorphosis seu transformatio unius speciei in aliam, quae idem quiddam esset cum creatione. Cujus enim potentiae est creare, ejusdem etiam est destruere, & convertere in aliam essentiam. Dei autem autem solius est cre-are.Dei ergo solius est rerum Metamorphosis, qualis est aquae in vinum & uxoris Lothi in statuam salis. Quod si metamorphosi Satanica homo essentialiter secundum formā transmutaretur, nec quidem externa species & materia hominis maneret. Nam materia & formae internae & speciei externae subjectum est. Jam ergo cū sua Adamo constiterit externa facies & materia, etiam tum, cum jam in peccatum prolapsus esset, forma etiam incolumis permanserit, necesse est. Inter Adamum itaque in statu inte-gritatis & statu corruptionis non essentiale sed accidentale discrimen est, seu homo renatus nec numero, nec specie, nec gene-re á se ipso non renato differt, quod ad substantiam attinet, hoc est, non est nova species, sed idem ipse subjectum est tum justitiae tum injustitiae vicissim. At ex illorum delirio Diabolus essentiali-ter transformavit animam rationalem hominis: quod quid, quae-so, aliud est quam ex specie prima effecisse aliam novam, & quod hinc omnino consequitur, esse molitorem seu fabricatorem & principium substantiae vitiosae? Quod vero excusant se, cum di-cunt hominem integrum & corruptum tota specie differre, non se vel-le id in physiologicus verum esse, sed id tantum locum habere in Theo-logia: pulcella profecto & bella excusatio est, & egregium ad sa-nandam causam elegantissimae distinctionis pharmacon. Video-or mihi hic audire quendam, qui sic diceret: Haec definitio, Homo est animal rationale, in Philosophia vera est, in Theologia falsa, ubi de ψυχικῷ, hoc est, brutali homine, ut interpretantur isti, agitur. Sed δ brutum pecus. Talésne inveniri homines, qui hominem ex homine tollunt, & quod semper & ubique verum & ἀμεταπλάστως ἀ-μεταπλάστον [?] est, ac re unum, hic verum, illic falsum, modo hoc, modo aliud esse arbitrantur? Quasi vero Theologia proponat nobis alias substantiarum & rerum creatarum species quàm philosophia, & non magis nos erudiat de corruptione & reparatione earundem substantiarum, quæ à Deo productæ sunt, & nullo alio. Qui ergo homo est in Physica, idem certè etiam homo erit in Theologia, & eum hominem, quem Christus redemit, non alium quàm Physicum fuisse credimus. Aliud autem est, cum dicimus, duplicem esse unius hominis respectum, unum Physi-cum, alterum Theologicum, & Philosophiam aliter judicare & definire hominem justum, quàm Theologiam: sed hoc ab [illegible, ~3 letters] hominis plurimum distat. Hominis itaque definitio philosophi-ca, qua dicitur esse animal rationis particeps, non evadit falsa in Theologia, etsi statuatur ratio in divinis esse vel depravatissima. Quo fit, ut etiam divus Athanasius hominem Christum, quà homo, animal esse rationis compos, contra hæreticos asserat, & à vero multum dissideat, si dicatur, Caro Christi esse longè alius veritatis, definitionis aut speciei, quàm nostra: cum re ipsa, asserente D. Cyrillo cum scriptura, Corpus quamvis λόγῳ proprium nostris tamen sit cognatum & consubstantiale, secundùm quod caro intelligitur. Videmur hactenus pro nostra virili arma ad-versaria retudisse, & vitiosam Peccati fabricam labefactasse. Sed tamen antequam dicendi finem faciamus, [illegible, ~7 letters] adjiciemus quædam ἀξιώματα ad verā [?] ἀληθείᾳ [?] cōparata. Primo principiū in-dubitatæ veritatis est de Transcendentib. & formæ unitate. ENS & unum convertuntur: neque enim speciērum confusio est. Et uni subjecto duæ formæ essentiales tribui nequeunt. Hoc tanquam ariete prosternitur hoc ex opinionum Manichæorum portentis unum, quod duæ sint in homine præsertim renato distincta forma, altera bona á Deo, altera mala á Diabolo. Et istud Illyrici: In homine renato peccatum originis esse substantialem imaginem. Dein-de certum est: In accurata doctrina & constituendis dogmatis non fas esse Subiectum adhibere loco generis, id quod & in Topica Aristotelis doctrina cavetur. Ut igitur in reprehensionem incurrit definitio: Febris est calor naturalis mutatus in igneum calorem: Sic vitio non vacat haec: Peccatum originis est natura hominis corrupta, &c. Addo tertium, quod haftenus nemo quidem (quod ego sciam) in dubium vocavit: Quicquid separa-ri potest ab uno subjecto, id non potest esse essentia alterius sub-jecti: seu quicquid est accidens in unare, id non potest esse pars substantiæ alterius: ut quia nigror est accidens in homine, non est essentialis corvo, sed inest ei κατὰ συμβεβηκός[?]. Quia igitur peccatum nunc congenitum ante lapsum hominis à corde abfuit, & post hanc vitam separabitur, ut accidens: non potest in hoc praesente hominis statu ipsa anima, ipsa substantia intelle-ctus & vo-luntatis, ipsum denique cor esse. Ad extremum, Bonū est æquale ENTI, hoc est, Bonum & essentia convertuntur, canon est Platonicorum & BONAVENTURÆ, quo nihil verius, nihil in Scholis decantatius. Et Omnis Natura, in quantum natura, bo-num est, quia opus Dei est. At peccatum nunquam fuit, nunquam est, nunquam erit bonum: semper fuit, semper est, semper deniq; erit malum, necessitate definitionis & Demonstrationis immutabili, cum illud sit ordinis & operis divini pollutio ac perversio, & labes deformissima, boniqúe privatio & corruptio. Hinc ergo concicitur, Peccatum ipsam hominis essentiam esse, vere dici non posse. Atq; haec quidem adhuc ἐκ τῶν ὑπαρχόντων[?], pro praesenti copia, remotis omnibus fucis & coloribus, ne auditore aurium voluptate delinire potius quàm veritate imbuere videremur. Ea autem adeò firma sunt, ut nullis contrariorum argumento-rum, quæ speciem gravitatis habet, machinis dimoveri, nedum leviùm ratiuncularum flabellis agitari posse existimem. Concludimus itaque cum D. Augustino: Natura humana, etsi mala est, quia vitiata est: non tamen malum est, quia natura est, sine quo bono nullum potest esse vitium:
units.tr: Thus they reason: Man is a sinner. The form of a sinner is sin. Therefore man is sin; and conversely, sin is the form of man. But in what school have they learned to argue like this? Is it the logic of folly or of wisdom? These men are fools. The form of a fool is folly. Therefore these men are sheer folly? Let Echo answer for me. What comes of a badly refuted argument? Nothing: that is, no syllogism. But, they say, this follows rightly from the rule taught in Aristotle's doctrine, which precedes the Categories: when one thing is said of another as of a subject, whatever is said of the predicate will also be said of the subject. Not at all. The rule remains true, but the example does not fit it. The motion of the Sun is always regular in the heavens, where it serves as a clock that never fails, even though a stupid sexton does not set the church clock correctly to the course of the Sun. But why does the example not fit the rule? Because it suffers from the fault of a faulty minor premise, or of the elenchus [ἔλεγχος ὅρων], that is, of the explanation of terms. So here you will find, as it were, loose brooms. For who is so leaden in logic as not to see that there are four terms: Man, Sinner, Form of a sinner, Sin? They pant and sweat greatly to extricate themselves, lest they seem to confess that the Devil is the creator and principle of evil substances, but in vain. For with the principles they use, the reef of the Manichaean dogma cannot be avoided. And here it happens to them especially as to those who stick in the mire: while they strive to lift one foot to free themselves, they plant the other deeper. They affirm that one and the same substance can have two most different authors, one the true creator God, the other the destroyer Devil, and yet that it is one thing in number. They offer this example: a good tree, when it is changed into a bad one, is not two trees but one; yet the cause of the good tree is one, and the cause of the bad tree is another. So they say; but how has this helped them? Is the bad tree, which is a bad tree, the tree itself, just as they say sin is a bad soul? A bad tree does not simply signify a tree, but a tree with an inhering quality, which is changeable. And when a good tree becomes a bad one, the same tree is the subject of both qualities, and this change or destruction does not produce a new substance of the tree, but a variation or alteration. Nor does the tree have two authors, one from whom the good is produced and another from whom the bad is produced. If by "destroyer" they meant the cause of a certain alteration, it could be conceded. For an altering cause is not a generating or creating cause, just as a man who mends a garment is a renewer, not a producer of it. The cause that heats water, like fire, is not the author of the substance of the water, since in alteration the subject remains the same and only a new quality is given to it. How, then, can such an altering destroyer be called the author of the substance itself? But they understand the destroyer as the creator, since they say that man unregenerate is the work of the Devil and the image of Satan, and they do not want the destruction in man to be some accident. Finally, they transfer to this the saying of Aristotle: the perishing of one thing is the rising of another. Then they say: why could a demon not be an effective cause of substance, since there are countless things which make substances out of other substances? For the cook, cooking meat in a pot, makes air out of water; and the country woman, by the help of motion, can make butter from milk; and the vintner makes lees from water and the dregs of grapes. Why, then, could the Devil, skilled in many arts, not change the substance of man and produce a different one from the former? But because they use their eyes (as in Plautus), it is fair that we give them something for their eyes too. For it is most certain that the fallacy of taking a non-cause as a cause is being committed. That water becomes air or vapour when it is heated over the fire is certainly not the work of man but of nature: it is the fire that penetrates, separates, thins, rarefies and digests all the parts of the water into vapour, while man merely applies and joins these natural agents, and is their servant in the action. So it is nature that makes the lees, with man merely assisting and mixing the water and the juice of the grape's refuse, so that these two become one: the grape. So the physician who cures [illegible] does not make flesh in the human body, but the remaining nature, which is restored, and the nourishment itself through the medicines, which are natural things. So when the big-breasted Nisa makes cheese from milk, granted that cheese is a new substance, since it is really the work of alteration, not generation, like imperfectly formed bodies or most meteors, yet that work is not the work of big-breasted Nisa or brawny Phyllis, but of nature. For in the milk there is nature and an internal principle, so that cheese can be made from it. Man merely adds instruments, such as a stick, by which the separation of the fatty and thin parts is accomplished, and by which coagulation, drying and hardening are effected. So man is not [illegible] the maker of that compound which is called salt, but nature, by the aid of art, draws salt out of salt water, which is present in that water. So what the chemists and alchemists say about [illegible] and [illegible], that through that wonderful stone which they call the Philosophers' Stone, rightly and accurately prepared, all metals can be converted into gold, and the inferior ones, that is, all metals except gold, can be transmuted into silver: to this it is truly answered that in that red stone, by which gold is said to be made, and in that white one, by which silver is said to be made, there is no power of truly converting metals, since it has no power of tinging except by way of a mixture, and artificial gold is nothing other than a mixed mass, or a metallic compound (the same judgement is to be made of artificial silver), as Claudius Triuncurianus rightly judges. We grant, he says, that the parts of these stones, most accurately prepared, [illegible] to the most subtle parts of that molten metal into which they are cast, so that a kind of metallic compound is made. For if metal is nothing other than watery earth congealed by great cold, which therefore cannot be restored to its former fluidity except by great heat, it is no wonder that gold and silver can be made one by mixing, especially when gold powder most accurately prepared is thrown into molten silver. Therefore it is made ONE by MIXTURE, not one by generation. Accordingly the form of gold remains in the matter and parts of gold, just as the form of silver remains in the matter of silver, no differently than in a mixture, as in wine diluted with water, or mixed with water, the form of both wine and water remains. So for the Devil, as for man and for art, which is a habit in man, a change into another, that is a metamorphosis or transformation of one species into another, would be the same thing as creation. For whoever has the power to create has also the power to destroy and convert into another essence. But the creating of things belongs to God alone. The metamorphosis of things therefore belongs to God alone, such as the change of water into wine and of Lot's wife into a pillar of salt. But if man were essentially transformed in form by a Satanic metamorphosis, not even the external appearance and matter of man would remain. For matter and internal form and external species are a single subject. Since, then, the external face and matter remained with Adam, it is necessary that the form also remained intact, even when he had already fallen into sin. Therefore between Adam in the state of integrity and Adam in the state of corruption there is no essential but only an accidental difference; or rather, the regenerate man does not differ from himself unregenerate in number, in species or in genus, as far as substance is concerned: that is, he is not a new species, but the same subject, now of righteousness, now of unrighteousness, in turn. But from the delirium of those men, the Devil essentially transformed the rational soul of man: what, I ask, is this other than to have made from the first species another, new one; and what necessarily follows from this, that he is the builder or fabricator and principle of a vicious substance? As for their excuse, when they say that integral man and corrupt man differ in whole species, and that they do not wish this to be true in physiology, but that it holds only in theology: that is indeed a pretty and fine excuse, and an excellent remedy, with an elegant distinction, for healing their cause. I seem to hear someone here who would say: This definition, man is a rational animal, is true in philosophy, false in theology, where the discussion concerns the psychical, that is, brutal, man, as these men interpret it. But this is a brutish herd. Are there really such men who remove man from man, and who think that what is always and everywhere true, and unchanging [ἀμεταπλάστως], and one and the same in reality, is true here and false there, now this, now that? As if theology set before us other species of substances and created things than philosophy does, and did not teach us more about the corruption and restoration of the same substances, which were produced by God and by no other. So what man is in physics, certainly the same man will be in theology too, and we believe that the man whom Christ redeemed was none other than the physical man. But it is one thing when we say that there is a twofold respect of one man, one physical, the other theological, and that philosophy judges and defines man otherwise than theology does; but this is very far from the [illegible] of man. Therefore the philosophical definition of man, by which he is said to be a partaker of reason, does not become false in theology, even if reason be held to be most depraved in divine matters. Hence also the divine Athanasius, against the heretics, asserts that Christ as man is an animal endowed with reason, and it is far from the truth to say, that the flesh of Christ is of a quite different truth, definition or species from ours: since in fact, as Cyril affirms with Scripture, the body, though proper to the Word [λόγῳ], is nonetheless akin and consubstantial with ours, insofar as it is understood as flesh. Thus far we seem, for our part, to have beaten back the adversary's arms and to have shaken the faulty fabric of Sin. But before we make an end of speaking, we shall add some axioms agreed upon for the sake of the truth [ἀληθείᾳ]. The first principle of indubitable truth concerns the transcendentals and the unity of form: BEING and ONE are convertible; for there is no confusion of species. Nor can two essential forms be attributed to one subject. By this ram is overthrown that one monstrosity of the Manichaean opinions, that in man, especially the regenerate, there are two distinct forms, one good, from God, the other evil, from the Devil. And likewise that saying of Illyricus: In the regenerate man, original sin is a substantial image. Next, it is certain that in accurate teaching and in setting out doctrines it is not permissible to put a subject in place of a genus, which is also guarded against in the doctrine of Aristotle's Topics. Just as the definition is open to censure: Fever is natural heat changed into fiery heat; so this one is not free from fault: Original sin is the corrupted nature of man, etc. I add a third point, which so far no one (as far as I know) has called in question: whatever can be separated from one subject cannot be the essence of another subject; or, whatever is an accident in one thing cannot be a part of the substance of another: as blackness is an accident in a man, it is not essential to a raven, but inheres in it per accidens [κατὰ συμβεβηκός]. Therefore, since the sin that is now congenital was not from the heart before the fall of man, and after this life will be separated, as an accident, it cannot be that in the present state of man the soul itself, the very substance of the understanding and will, or the heart itself, is sin. Finally, Good is equal to Being: that is, Good and Essence are convertible; this is the canon of the Platonists and of Bonaventure, than which nothing is truer and nothing more often sung in the schools. And every nature, as nature, is good, because it is the work of God. But sin never was good, is not good, and never will be good; it always was, always is, and always will be evil, by the unchangeable necessity of definition and demonstration, since it is a pollution and perversion of the order and work of God, a most hideous stain, and a privation and corruption of good. Hence it is concluded that Sin cannot truly be said to be the very essence of man. And these things, for the present, are drawn from what is at hand [ἐκ τῶν ὑπαρχόντων], with all pretences and colours set aside, lest we seem to soothe the ears of the hearer with pleasure rather than to imbue him with truth. Moreover they are so firm that I think they cannot be moved by any engines of contrary arguments, which have the appearance of weight, much less be stirred by the fans of lighter little reasonings. We conclude, therefore, with Saint Augustine: Human nature, although it is evil because it has been vitiated, is nevertheless not evil because it is nature, without which good there can be no vice.

units.la: Et quanquam veteris labes innata veneni Tam procul insedit carni, tam fixa profundis Natura in gremio radicibus haret, ut instar Morbida fermenti vires penetraverit omnes Corporis atq; animae, medijs diffusa medullis: Non tamen arbitrium est, non est substantia cordis.
units.tr: Although the innate poison of the ancient fall has lodged so deep in the flesh, and clings so firmly to the roots of nature in its inmost core, that, like the morbid force of leaven, it has penetrated all the powers of body and soul, spreading through their innermost marrow, yet it is not the will, and it is not the substance of the heart.

units.la: Nec est in omnibus praedicamentis seu Transcendens, ut F. scripsit: Sed est in genere eorum, quae accidunt homini praeter essentiam, ut morbus, qui est affectus παρὰ φύσιν [?]: Ac, ut explicatius dicam, est 1. στέρησις [?], hoc est, privatio conformitatis cum aeterna & immota norma justitiae divinae in lege expressae, ignoratio Dei, dubitationes de Deo, diffidentia, aversio voluntatis à Deo. 2. ἀνάγκη [?], ad efficienda ea praestandaq;, quae descripta in lege Dei rigidissime à toto humano genere exiguntur. 3. ὁρμή [?] seu inclinatio propensioq;, imò ὁρμή [?], id est, incitatio & impulsus ad vagos & errantes motus lege Dei prohibitos. Est itaq; hominis naturae vitiatio, seu corruptio talis, qua natura evadit mala, non MA-lum [?] ipsum, quod potissimum & πρῶτος in mente intelligente & voluntate appetente ac libera inhaeret.
units.tr: Nor is it one of the categories, or a transcendental, as F. has written. It belongs to the genus of those things that befall a man beyond his essence, like a disease, which is an affection contrary to nature [παρὰ φύσιν]. To explain it more fully: it is (1) privation [στέρησις], that is, the lack of conformity with the eternal and unchanging norm of divine justice expressed in the law; ignorance of God, doubts about God, distrust, and the turning away of the will from God. (2) Necessity [ἀνάγκη], that is, the need to perform those things which the law of God, described most strictly, demands from the whole human race. (3) Impulse [ὁρμή], or inclination and propensity, indeed an urging [ὁρμή], that is, an incitement and push towards wandering and erring motions, which the law of God forbids. It is therefore a vitiation, or corruption, of human nature, by which nature becomes evil; not evil itself, which chiefly and first [πρῶτος] inheres in the intelligent mind and the appetitive, free will.

units.la: Hæc habui, quae de horribili labe vitii originalis strictim dicerem, & ut sacrorum studiosos ad Philosophiae studium excitarem, & abusum ejus cavendum monerem. Est enim vera Philosophia lux naturalis animis à Deo in creatione insita (cujus radii aliqui etiam in natura miserè sauciata contaminataq; remanserunt) & organon Spiritus divini ad erudiendum & convincendum de veritate omnes non insanos, aut petulanter adversa fronte ei repugnantes. Nam ratio à Spiritu sancto ad divinas res percipiendas illustrata, per coelestis doctrinae vocem, & ex πρώτοις atq; axiomatis in scriptura Prophetica & Apostolica traditis, secundum normas bonæ & necessariæ consecutionis divinitus rationis compoti creaturæ impressas, considerat & judicat, quomodo partes doctrinæ inter se aptæ colligataéq; sint, atq; cohæreant, quomodo se mutuo stabiliant, quid illis ἀκόλουθον ac consentaneum, quid ab iisdem sit dissentaneum & alienum. Hanc rationis συνεχείας & usum in divinis rebus tantum abest, ut Deus improbet, ut illum etiam severissimé requirat. Quid? quòd propter hunc usum naturam intelligentem condidit, ac ἡγεμονικὴν [?] seu normas judicandi & discernendi verum à falso, certum ab incerto, illi insevit, ut, quæ mens & voluntas ipsius sit, probare ac confirmare, & obloquentes convincere possit. Et sicut inter sobriam veramq; Philosophiam, quæ à nævis & erroribus vindicata ac repurgata, se ut famulã dominæ Theologiæ addicit, ita, ut nec extraordinaria Dei opera ordinariis naturæ operibus evertat, nec commenta & monstrosa hominum mendacia, pugnantia cū immota veritate Verbo & natura Dei, absolutæ omnipotentiæ Dei titulo ac τεχνήματα venditari permittat: Inter hanc igitur Sapientiam, & inter sacram Scripturam, ut re ipsa non est contradictio: nec, quod in Philosophia verum est, id continuò in Theologia est mendacium: sic etiam τέταρτον διδάξεως, hoc est, rationem & formam res explicandi, demonstrandi, & refellendi aliam non servat Theosophia, nisi quam sana Philosophia monstrat.
units.tr: I have said these things briefly about the dreadful stain of original sin, both to stir students of the sacred writings to the study of philosophy and to warn them to beware its abuse. For true philosophy is the natural light implanted in souls by God at creation (some rays of which remain even in nature grievously wounded and polluted), and it is the instrument of the Holy Spirit for teaching and convincing of the truth all who are not mad or who do not wantonly oppose it with a hostile brow. For reason, illumined by the Holy Spirit to perceive divine things through the voice of heavenly doctrine, and from the first principles and axioms handed down in the prophetic and apostolic Scripture, according to the norms of good and necessary consequence divinely impressed on the reasoning of the creature, considers and judges how the parts of doctrine fit together and cohere, how they mutually support one another, what agrees and is consistent with them, and what dissents from them and is foreign to them. God is so far from disapproving this sequence of reasoning and its use in divine things that he demands it most strictly. Why, indeed, did he create an intelligent nature for this very use, and implant in it the governing faculty [ἡγεμονικὴ], that is, the norms for judging and distinguishing truth from falsehood and certainty from uncertainty, so that it may be able to prove and confirm what its own mind and will is, and to convict those who contradict it? And just as sober and true philosophy, cleansed and purged of blemishes and errors, submits itself as a handmaid to her mistress, theology, so that neither extraordinary works of God overturn the ordinary works of nature, nor human inventions and monstrous lies, at odds with the unchanging truth of God's Word and nature, are hawked under the title of God's absolute omnipotence and as contrivances: so between this wisdom and the sacred Scripture there is, in fact, no contradiction. What is true in philosophy is not therefore straightaway a lie in theology. Likewise, the fourth element of teaching, that is, the reason and form of explaining, demonstrating and refuting things, is not observed by theosophy except as sound philosophy shows it.

units.la: Sicut itaq; (ut ad hypothesin descendamus) Logica est instrumentum verum à falso discernendi in Philosophia, sic & in Theologia. Sicut omnis doctrina Philosophica, quæ demonstratione constituitur & absolvitur, exsistit ex principiis: ita etiam doctrina cœlestis habet sua τὰ πρῶτα ἀναπόδεικτα & αὐτότητα, e quibus demonstrationes Theologicæ conficiuntur. Res quidem ipsas & principia Theologica non gignit Philosophia: sed ut Theologus ex iis aliquid exstruere possit, non aliam quàm Philosophicam amussim adhibet.
units.tr: Therefore, just as (to come down to the hypothesis) logic is the instrument for distinguishing the true from the false in philosophy, so it is also in theology. Just as all philosophical doctrine, which is constituted and completed by demonstration, rests on principles, so heavenly doctrine too has its own first things which are indemonstrable [τὰ πρῶτα ἀναπόδεικτα] and self-evident [αὐτότητα], from which theological demonstrations are built. Philosophy does not generate the things themselves and the theological principles; but in order that the theologian may construct something from them, he uses no other rule than the philosophical one.

units.la: Abusus autem Philosophiae est, cum obtentu sive hujus sive theologiae suscipiuntur διαθέσεις[?] contrariae principiis seu anticipatis notionibus theologicis, & finguntur falsa principia, atque ex his dogmata cuduntur & defensantur cum veritate philosophica & theologica pugnantia: aut alioquin veris principiis & inde exstructis veris complexionibus multa per malam consecutionem affluuntur. Cum Philosophia fingitur sufficere ad docendos homines de Deo, ejus cultu, & hominum salute: (sicut olim Doctor quidam, audiente Melanchthone, dixit, etiam amissis libris propheticis & apostolicis satis doceri posse Ecclesiam ex Ethicis Aristoteleis) cum dogmata Ecclesiæ rationi ignota deducuntur non ex divinis oraculis, sed ex rationibus philosophicis, abusus philosophiæ est. Cum, quæ philosophia de rebus sibi subjectis recte pronunciat, ad res divinas extenduntur, ad quas minime congruunt (ut cum politica justitia ad Evangelicam transfertur) abusus philosophiæ est, & confusio cum Theologia detestanda. Cum opiniones aut locutiones, quæ, etiam in rebus philosophicis usurpatæ, sunt incertæ, impropriæ, ambiguæ, obscuræ, & subtilitatis otiosæ, transferuntur ad res Theologicas, quæ illis involuuntur, & in pugnas disceptationum inutiles convertuntur, (sicut Flacius in doctrina de hominis depravatione disputans de formis substantialibus, & an in corruptione substantiali fiat resolutio usque ad materiam primam, simplicissimam doctrinam de peccato originis in labyrinthos conjicit) aut cum distinctiones, appellationes & phrases Philosophicæ alieno sensu, & novis ambiguitatibus sermonis vafre excogitatis usurpantur in doctrina Ecclesiæ ad eludendum argumenta & testimonia objecta, ad quærenda effugia, & circumveniendos eos, qui insolens sermonis genus non intelligunt, hic pernitiosus philosophiæ & rationis abusus est, Sophistarum ματαιοτεχνία[?] est, unde iterum piscatoria doctrinæ & dictionis Apostolicæ simplicitas involvitur, & perplexa redditur, ut hodie multi Ecclesiæ doctores ad κυρίας δόξας [?] confirmandas abutuntur Philosophicis distinctionibus diversorum modorum & respectuum.
units.tr: But the abuse of philosophy occurs when, under the pretext of either philosophy or theology, dispositions [διαθέσεις] contrary to theological principles or preconceived notions are adopted, false principles are invented, and from these dogmas are coined and defended which clash with philosophical and theological truth; or when, otherwise, from true principles and true combinations built upon them, many errors are drawn by faulty inference. It is an abuse of philosophy when it is claimed that philosophy suffices to teach people about God, his worship, and the salvation of men (as a certain teacher once said in Melanchthon's hearing, that even with the prophetic and apostolic books lost, the Church could be sufficiently taught from the Ethics of Aristotle). It is an abuse of philosophy when dogmas of the Church that are unknown to reason are deduced not from the divine oracles but from philosophical arguments. It is an abuse of philosophy, and a confusion with theology to be detested, when what philosophy rightly pronounces about its own subjects is extended to divine things, to which it does not fit at all (as when political justice is transferred to the Gospel). It is this pernicious abuse of philosophy and reason when opinions or expressions, which even when used in philosophical matters are uncertain, improper, ambiguous, obscure and idle subtleties, are transferred to theological matters, which become entangled in them and are turned into useless battles of dispute. (So Flacius, disputing about the depravity of man, drew the simplest doctrine of original sin into labyrinths by discussing substantial forms, and whether in substantial corruption a resolution is made down to prime matter.) It is likewise such an abuse when philosophical distinctions, appellations and phrases are used in a foreign sense, and with new ambiguities of speech craftily devised, in the doctrine of the Church, to evade the arguments and testimonies brought against it, to seek escapes, and to circumvent those who do not understand this unfamiliar manner of speaking. This is the sophists' vain craft, [ματαιοτεχνία], by which the fishermen's simplicity of apostolic doctrine and speech is again enveloped and made perplexed, so that today many teachers of the Church abuse philosophical distinctions of different modes and respects to confirm their principal tenets [κυρίας δόξας].

units.la: Apparet ex his Flacium Philosophia abusum esse eo ipso, quòd dogma suum de Peccato è Philosophorum scholis deduxit, res ac doctrinas toto genere diversas cōfudit, ad figmentum denique cerebri sui doctrinam coelestem inflexit, & detorsit. Usus contrà legitimus rationis, & humanæ sapientiæ in rebus fidei est, cùm harmonia veritatis divinitus patefactæ retinetur, Philosophica dogmata ex suis, Theologica item ea, quæ supra lumen naturę & rationis sunt, ex suis & οἰκείοις principiis extruuntur, & explicantur: ea verò, quæ naturali etiam luce cernuntur, & rationi patent, & Theologicis & Philosophicis axiomatis probantur. Bonæ enim menti grata est confirmatio veritatis, ubi intelligit naturalem & Philosophicam notitiam cum coelesti voce conjunctam esse. Recte igitur & bene utimur Philosophia, cùm, si alicubi divinorum oraculorum, & rectæ rationis testimonia consentire videmus, hujus etiam judicium adhibemus. Germanus præterea Philosophiæ usus est, cum Theologia judicatur esse humanæ sapientiæ ἐπανόρθωμα [?] παρεπλήρωμα [?], hoc est, Philosophia per coelestem sapientiam corrigitur exorbitans, & completur deficiens, & secundum normas & metas artium judicandi de vero & falso, ac res explicandi, à Deo monstratas tàm sacra quàm profana tractantur & disputantur. Hos Philosophiæ usus concessos nobis & necessarios si quis in dubium vocat, proferat, si potest, vel unum ex augusto illo sacrarum rerum volumine argumentum, quod ad regulas bonæ consecutionis ab eruditis Philosophicis traditas non congruat, probet alium esse modum contexendi syllogismum, aut inveniendi media syllogistica in Theologia, quàm in Philosophia, sive media illa sint demonstrativa, sive probabilia: probet aliam esse rationem & methodum demonstrandi Theologica, quàm Philosophica. Una atq; eadem via est seu methodus ratiocinandi de omnibus quæquæstionibus ἢ[?] περὶ φιλοσοφίαν καὶ περὶ τέχνην ὁποιανοῦν[?] ἢ μάθημα, & ad Philosophiam & ad quamvis artem & disciplinam pertinenti- bus, inquit Aristoteles. Et Dialecticam nunquam Christiana doctrina reformidat, ait Augustinus. Quid multa? Ecclesia Dei Philosophicis literis semper fuit erudita, ut quæ sciret sine his veritatis propugnationem, pernitiosorum errorum explosionem, implicatarum rerum explicationem, difficillimarum & intricatarum quæstionum dissolutionem fieri non posse.
units.tr: From these things it appears that Flacius abused philosophy by the very fact that he deduced his dogma of sin from the schools of the philosophers, confused things and doctrines wholly different in kind, and finally bent and twisted heavenly doctrine into a figment of his own brain. The legitimate use of reason and of human wisdom in matters of faith is when the harmony of divinely revealed truth is preserved: philosophical dogmas are built and explained from their own principles, and likewise those theological things which lie above the light of nature and reason, from their own proper principles; but those things which are discerned even by natural light and lie open to reason are proved both by theological and by philosophical axioms. For confirmation of the truth is welcome to a good mind, when it understands that natural and philosophical knowledge is joined with the heavenly voice. So we use philosophy rightly and well, when, if we see the testimonies of divine oracles and of right reason agreeing somewhere, we also apply philosophy's judgement. Moreover, there is a German use of philosophy, when theology is judged to be the correction [ἐπανόρθωμα] and the completion [παρεπλήρωμα] of human wisdom, that is, when philosophy, going astray, is corrected by heavenly wisdom, and what is deficient is completed; and when sacred and profane matters, shown by God, are treated and disputed according to the norms and limits of the arts for judging truth and falsehood and for explaining things. If anyone calls these uses of philosophy, which are granted and necessary to us, into doubt, let him produce, if he can, even one argument from that august volume of sacred things which does not agree with the rules of good consequence laid down by the learned philosophers; let him prove that there is another way of constructing a syllogism, or of finding syllogistic middle terms, in theology than in philosophy, whether those middle terms are demonstrative or probable; let him prove that there is another manner and method of demonstrating theological matters than philosophical ones. There is one and the same way or method of reasoning about all questions, whether concerning philosophy or any art whatever [περὶ φιλοσοφίαν καὶ περὶ τέχνην ὁποιανοῦν], or discipline, and it pertains both to philosophy and to any art and discipline, says Aristotle. And Christian doctrine never shrinks from dialectic, says Augustine. Why say more? The Church of God has always been instructed in philosophical letters, since it knew that without them the defence of truth, the blasting of pernicious errors, the explanation of tangled matters, and the resolution of very difficult and intricate questions cannot be accomplished.

units.la: Tanta igitur cum sit Philosophiæ commoditas, in ea studiosi se diligenter exercebunt, nec adolescentuli statim, ut in publicam scholam venerunt, in sacra illotis manibus & pedibus, & tanquam sus, quod dicitur, in rosetum irruent, nullam prorsus vel certe admodum tenuem scientiam & usum nostrarum literarum habentes. AEmulabuntur potius hos præsentes candidatos, qui in superiorum facultatum arcem, non involare, sed gradatim conscendere cupiunt, non arroganter & superbe despicientes Philosophicorum studiorum & honorum gradus à majoribus nostris institutos. Ut enim ad Romani Capitolii fastigium ascensurus ante intermedios gradus percurrebat, quàm ad summum perveniret[?]: Sic sapiens antiquitas voluit, cum, qui ad studiorum suorum finem volet aspirare, per singulas artes, tanquam per gradus decurrere, quo demum curiu[?] confecto, extremo studiorum bono potiretur.
units.tr: Since philosophy is so useful, students will apply themselves to it diligently. Young men, as soon as they come into the public school, should not rush straight into sacred studies with unwashed hands and feet, as the saying goes, like a pig into a rose garden, having no knowledge or use of our literature, or at most a very slight one. Rather, they should imitate these present candidates, who wish to climb to the citadel of the higher faculties step by step rather than fly there, and who do not arrogantly and proudly scorn the degrees and honours of philosophical study established by our forebears. For just as one who is about to climb to the summit of the Roman Capitol passes through the intermediate steps before reaching the top, so wise antiquity wished that whoever aspires to the goal of his studies should run through the individual arts as through steps, so that when the course is finished he may at last attain the highest good of learning.

units.la: HOC cum intelligerent hi 23. adolescentes, hactenus omne suum otium, curas, & cogitationes omnes in Logicis, utraq; lingua, & initiis Mathescos defixerunt, & cum ab honestissimo nostro Collegio primum suorum studiorum testimonium peterent, ab eo auditi sunt, mores, vita & eruditio eorum explorata diligenter. Ac quidem ab exploratione illa digni judicati sunt, in quos publice prima laurea conferretur: quam ob rem etiam eos in hoc theatrum produximus. Sed cum non parum referat, omnibus liquido constare eos esse tales, quibus honos decretus merito meritò tribuatur, antequam ornetur, & tanquam dii minorum gentium prodantur, specimen quoddam eruditionis suae singuli edent. Primus ergo problema tuum clarè edisserito. Deinde caeteri singulatim suas quaestiones explicanto.
units.tr: When these 23 young men understood this, they have hitherto devoted all their leisure, care and thought to logic, in both languages, and to the rudiments of mathematics. When they sought from our most honourable College the first testimony of their studies, they were heard by it, and their morals, life and learning were carefully examined. Indeed, those were judged worthy of that examination to whom the first laurel is to be conferred publicly, and for this reason we have also brought them out into this theatre. But since it matters not a little that it be clearly established to everyone that they are such men as deserve the honour decreed to them, each of them will give a specimen of his learning before they are adorned and presented like minor gods. Let the first one therefore clearly expound his problem. Then let the others explain their questions one by one.
Each of them delivered his short declamation.

units.la: Audistis, ut hi studiosis[?] adolescentes in amplissimo hoc consensu clarissimorum & ornatissimorum virorum, sui periculum fecerint, ut ingenii & eruditionis specimen dederint, quod vobis probari non dubito. Restat igitur, ut eos Philosophiae Baccalaureos renunciem. Sed tamen antequam hoc fiat, jurejurando se astringent, nihil se contra dignitatem hujus inclytae Academiae, & contra honorem Professorum Philosophiae praeceptorum suorum commissuros unquam, & hos honores nusquam unquam iterum petituros, & si qua alia capita sunt. Jurejurando igitur optimi candidati vos obligabitis, invocato vero & vivo Deo teste & judice, si contra unquam, quod absit, feceritis. Recita nomenclator formulam juris jurandi.
units.tr: You have heard how these young students, in this very large assembly of most distinguished and accomplished men, have made trial of themselves and given a specimen of their talent and learning, which I do not doubt will please you. It remains, then, for me to proclaim them Bachelors of Philosophy. But before this is done, they will bind themselves by oath that they will never commit anything against the dignity of this famous Academy or against the honour of the Professors of Philosophy, their teachers, and that they will never again seek these honours anywhere, and whatever other points there are. You, best candidates, will bind yourselves by this oath, calling on the living God as witness and judge, should you ever act against it, which God forbid. Herald, recite the formula of the oath.

units.la: Recitata est formula, & singuli tactis sceptris jurárunt.
units.tr: The formula was recited, and each, touching the sceptres, swore.
PROCLAMATION.

units.la: Ego igitur Rodolphus Goclenius, non tam meo, quàm universi Collegii Professorum Philosophiae nomine, in amplissimo hoc consessu, & universae Academiae conspectu, renunctio & declaro hos 25.[?] adolescentes ex aequo Philosophiae Baccalaureos. Quod illis felix, faustum, & bonum Deus Opt.Max. esse velit.
units.tr: I, therefore, Rudolph Goclenius, in the name not so much of myself as of the whole College of Professors of Philosophy, in this most distinguished assembly and in the sight of the whole Academy, proclaim and declare these 25 young men equally Bachelors of Philosophy. May God, the Best and Greatest, will that this be happy, fortunate and good for them.
The insignia is bestowed and explained.

units.la: Addidit huic gradui sapiens Vetustas symbolum, & insigne, sertum laureum: sicut nulli unquam actus solennes apud ullos populos fuerunt sine aliqua ceremoniarum & symbolorum solennitate. Notis enim illis hoc voluerunt significari, quod agitur, & perpetuae quasi memoriae pignus tradi. Quorsum ergo laurea illa corolla? Dicam equidem breviter, & nihil παρὰ μέλος[?]. Laurus arbor intonso Apollini sacra fuit, quia ἀειθαλής[?], hoc est, perpetuo viret, & in Parnasso monte Musis sacro felicissimè succrevit, ut scribit Plinius. In eam fingitur pulcerrima virgo Daphne, Apollinem, qui in eam exardesceret, fugiens, esse conversa. Quàm pulcrum hic veritatis involucrum? Virtus enim & eruditio adeptu & tanquam captu quidem difficiles sunt, & amatores suos saepe fugiunt: sed aeternum & perpetuum, ac nunquam marcescens ex illis nomen est. Fuit etiam laurus propter perpetuum suum virorem & vigorem apud Romanos insigne triumpi & lætitiæ,& ornamentum augustarum,hoc est,Pontificiarum ac principalium ædium,&triumphatorum,qui in Capitolium deducebantur, gestatis in capite laureis coronis,quas in sinum Jovis deponerent. Monebuntur igitur Baccalaurei nostri, se hostes doctrinæ & virtutis aliqua ex parte superasse, & Jehovæ pro felici successu laborum gratias agendas. Præterea cum laurus sit arbor odoratissima, ut eruditionis & honestatis ornamentum non immeritò adhibetur. Non aliunde enim, quàm ex eruditione cum humanitate & suavibus moribus copulata, suaviores exhalant & afflantur odores. Huc ergo ocyus contendite cum lepidis & rotundis vestris capitulis, ut honoris & laudis vestræ insigne, quisque suum auferatis.
units.tr: Wise antiquity added to this degree a symbol and insignia, the laurel wreath, just as no solemn acts among any peoples have taken place without some solemnity of ceremonies and symbols. For by such signs they wished to signify what is being done and to hand over, as it were, a pledge of perpetual memory. Why then a laurel crown? I shall answer briefly, and not out of tune [παρὰ μέλος]. The laurel was a tree sacred to the unshorn Apollo because it is ever-green [ἀειθαλής], that is, it flourishes perpetually, and on Mount Parnassus, sacred to the Muses, it grew most happily, as Pliny writes. It is fabled that the most beautiful virgin Daphne was changed into it while fleeing Apollo, who burned with love for her. How fine is this veil over the truth! For virtue and learning are difficult to obtain and, as it were, to seize, and often flee their lovers; but the name they bestow is eternal and perpetual and never fades. The laurel was also, on account of its perpetual greenness and vigour, among the Romans a sign of triumph and joy, and an ornament of the august, that is, of the pontifical and princely houses, and of the triumphers who were led up to the Capitol, wearing laurel wreaths on their heads, which they would lay down in the lap of Jove. Our Bachelors are therefore reminded that they have in some measure overcome the enemies of learning and virtue, and that thanks must be given to Jehovah for the happy outcome of their labours. Moreover, since the laurel is a most fragrant tree, it is not undeservedly used as an ornament of learning and honesty. For sweeter odours are breathed out and wafted forth from nothing but learning joined with courtesy and pleasant manners. Hasten therefore quickly, with your neat and round little caps, so that each of you may take away the insignia of his honour and praise.
I. Christophorus Cramerus of Allendorf.

units.la: AD stivam, si non capiat quem gloria Lauri, Nec super ipse sua molitur laude laborem: Tu vero ad doctam cathedram bene docte Cramere. Pro virtute tibi decus immortale repono Hoc Daphnes fertum. Virtutis calcar honores.
units.tr: If the glory of the laurel does not take hold of one who guides the plough, nor does he labour for his own praise, then you, well-taught Cramer, to the learned chair. For your virtue I lay before you this immortal honour, this garland of Daphne. Honours are the spur of virtue.
II. Melchior Colerus of Birstein.

units.la: NOn atro Colere mihi carbone notande, Hem viridem laurum tibi, præmia prima laborum. Discite ab hoc pueri: non qui certamina segnes Fugerunt, sed pugnarunt, meruêre Coronas. Arte petit summas vel Carbonarius arces.
units.tr: Colerus, not to be marked by me with black charcoal, behold the green laurel for you, the first prizes of labour. Boys, learn from this: those who did not shun contests out of idleness, but fought, have earned the crowns. By skill even the charcoal-burner reaches the highest heights.
III. Jodocus Pforrius of Kassel.

units.la: PRæmia[?] Jodoco jam nunc solvemus. E.ovemus, Quæ quisquis spernis, dispereas. E.pereas. Ut sat sis pulcer mihi Baccalaureus, E.aureus, En Jodoce tibi Laureola. E.aureola. Hanc reverenter[?] habe, casto quam pollice Clio Fecit: quo[?] hanc ardet te Galathea. E. [illegible, ~3 letters]
units.tr: Jodocus, we shall now pay you your prizes. Whoever you are, if you scorn them, may you perish, so that you may be a fine Baccalaureus for me, golden. See, Jodocus, your little laurel, a golden little garland. Hold it in reverence, which Clio made with a chaste thumb, with which Galatea burns for you. [illegible]
IIII. Wigandus Heimelius of Grenzebach.
To Heimelius I give a laurel; to Heimelius I give a little jewel.

units.la: Lusu, jocis & otio Non crescit eruditio. Labore Divi munera Mortalibus vendunt sua.
units.tr: Learning does not grow through play, jokes and idleness. By labour the gods sell their gifts to mortals.
V. Simon Lucanus of Neocuria.

units.la: UT decus est horto laurus, laurusq; corona, Pulcra corona coma, coma Nympha, Nympha chorea: Sic virtus arti decus est, artiq; juventa, Docta juventa Schola, schola templis, templa colonis. Hac tua te moneat laetissima laurea Simon.
units.tr: As the laurel is the ornament of the garden, and the laurel is a crown, a beautiful crown for hair, the hair for a nymph, the nymph for the dance: so virtue is an ornament to art, and art to youth, learned youth to the school, the school to temples, and temples to farmers. May this most joyful laurel admonish you, Simon.
VI. Philippus Halgans of Grünberg.

units.la: SAúlne inter vates? inter ferus anser olores? Non ita: doctrina est factus & arte ciéur. Ergò vola huc, &, ut orneris pulcrè, caput unum Da mihi: Praposito catera dono coco. Ad vigila libris: damnosa est alea pernox: In serto gemma est (ut placet?) ista tuo.
units.tr: Are you among the prophets? Among the wild geese, are you a swan? Not so: you are made and roused by learning and art. So fly here, and that you may be finely adorned, give me one head; I will give the rest to the Provost. Keep watch over your books: gambling through the night is ruinous. In your garland, this gem is (as it pleases?) yours.
VII. Theodorus de Ana of Geismar.

units.la: QUi Theodore colis praesignia dona Dei, artes, Immemor haud unquam nominis ipse tui, Te manet haec merces, proprio tibi adepta labore: Cuiq; sua est virtus, non aliena, decus.
units.tr: You, Theodore, who cultivate the outstanding gifts of God, the arts, never forgetful of your own name: this reward awaits you, won by your own labour. For each person's honour is his own virtue, not another's.
VIII. Michaël Lambertus of Geismar.

units.la: AT tibi nunc textam tribuo Lamberte corollam, Qua damnosi expers senii, tua tempora circum Floreat, aeternoq; nitens scintillet honore, Donec ad aequoreis ignotos fluctibus ignes Clara Ariadnea rutilabunt signa corona.
units.tr: But now to you, Lambert, I give a woven garland, free of harmful old age, which around your temples may flower and shine with eternal honour, until the bright signs of Ariadne's crown glitter with unknown fires over the sea waves.
IX. Joannes Curtius of Ziegenhain.

units.la: FLoribus his redimire caput, pulcerrime Curti, Intactis anui[?], tactis a virgine pulcra, Lectisq; in Charitum pictis & Apollinis hortis, Quam factum bene; namq; dedit tibi Gratia nomen.
units.tr: To crown your head with these flowers, most beautiful Curtius: untouched by old age, touched by a beautiful maiden, and picked from the painted gardens of the Graces and Apollo. How well it is made; for Grace gave you the name.
X. Nicolaus Lumhardus of Berstadt.

units.la: LUmharde adesto Laonice: te volo. Tibi hanc corollam Musa nexilem dedit, Carptam è virentis pratuli intonsa coma. Quo neq; protervum pastor unquam egit pecus, Neq; falcis unquam venit acies improba. Apis una flores veré libat aureos, Puris honestius quos rigat lymphis pudor.
units.tr: Lumhard, be present, Laonice: I want you. The Muse has given you this woven garland, plucked from the green meadow with unshorn hair, where the wanton shepherd never drove his flock, nor did the wicked edge of the sickle ever come. A single bee sips golden flowers in spring, which modesty waters with purer streams.
XI. Henricus Crugius of Kassel.

units.la: URcee, non hedera, mihi non cingende corymbis Thyrsigeri, (Musas sobria vita decet) Urcee, sed lauro Phoebi, castaq; Minervae Condecorande, artis pramia tolle tuae.
units.tr: Urcee, not with ivy clusters to be bound to me, bearer of the thyrsus (sober living befits the Muses), Urcee, but with Phoebus' laurel, and adorned for chaste Minerva, take the prizes of your art.
XII. Conradus Wrasen of Ziremberg.

units.la: WRase[?] praesenti cape letus hora Lauream: pulcro micat haec pyropo, Et levis cespes probat esse numen, Quod regit orbem.
units.tr: Wrase, take the laurel joyfully in this present hour: it gleams with a beautiful garnet, and the light turf proves it to be the divinity that rules the world.
XIII. Georgius Albinus of Giessen.

units.la: TV quoq; fer capitis decus hoc, Albine, corollam, Texuit hanc digitis Gratia terna suis. Si quos exercet Musarum cura laborque, Hos manet & merces debita laudis honos.
units.tr: You too, Albinus, bear this garland as an ornament for your head; three Graces wove it with their own fingers. If the care and labour of the Muses occupy anyone, for these the due honour of praise remains as reward.
XIIII. Johannes Mercator of Marburg.

units.la: HUc Mercator ades, sequitorq; trahentia fata: Ingenii merces merx erit ista tui.
units.tr: Come here, Mercator, and follow the fates that draw you: this will be the reward, the merchandise, of your talent.

units.la: Ars bona vi magna non est mercabilis auri,Illa sed in pigro parta labore venit.
units.tr: Good art is not bought for much gold; it is won by slow, painstaking labour.
XV. Laurentius Scheichius of Grünberg.

units.la: LAurentio debetur merito laurea, Huc ergo Scheichi, & hinc tuam fer lauream, Ex Gratiarum pratuli intonsa coma Aptam: probis, & his unis, quos auream Natura docuit ipsa temperantiam, Fas carpere illinc: improbis autem nefas. At tu fuscae Scheichi vinculum comae Amicè suscipe, quod pia dextra porrigit.
units.tr: Laurel is rightly owed to Laurentius. Come hither, then, Scheich, and bear your laurel from here, fitting, woven from the unshorn hair of the meadow of the Graces. It is lawful for the upright, and for those alone whom nature herself taught self-control, to pluck it from there; for the wicked it is unlawful. But you, Scheich, take in friendship the knot of your dusky hair, which a pious right hand offers.
XVI. Aegidius Keil of Eschwege.

units.la: UBi malignus nodus est, Quaerendus asper cuneus est: Nam cunei vis est maxima. Ingenium si sit plumbeum, Ut haereat fixissimis Radicibus scientia Animo tandem, unus cuneus est, Et alter, Diligentia, Et continuata Motio Cerebri, & crebra lectio. His, AEgidi, cuneis tibi Adeptus es hanc lauream. Sic perge, habebis auream.
units.tr: Where there is a stubborn knot, a sharp wedge must be sought: for the force of a wedge is greatest. If the mind is leaden, so that it may cling with the firmest roots of knowledge in the mind at last, one wedge is one thing, and another is diligence, and continued exercise of the brain, and frequent reading. With these wedges, Aegidius, you have obtained this laurel. Go on so, and you will have a golden one.
XVII. Bernhardus Breslerus of Marburg.

units.la: HUc ades, ursinum qui praefers nomine robur, Hac tegat ornatum laurus odora caput. Laurea frontis honos, tali quae Jaspide fulget, Cum natura usus perficit artis opus.
units.tr: Come here, you who bear the strength of the bear in your name: let fragrant laurel cover your adorned head. The laurel, the honour of the brow, which shines with such a jasper, when nature with art perfects the work.
XVIII. Johannes Hamel of Wolfhagen.

units.la: Si duo concurrant in aperti pulvere campi Forte viri, & posito vervecis pignore certent, Hunc theatro exponunt redimitum colla caput ve, Aut fronde aut serto viridi, hoc excussor habebit. Sic ego vervecem, sed nil rationis egentem, Flore coronabo viridi, sacrumq; dicabo, Wolf Hagiæ: Non est fas spernere munera Divum.
units.tr: If two men happen to meet on the dust of an open field and contend for a wager of a ram, they set the prize, and the one who shakes off the other will have it, crowned about the neck with a garland or a green wreath. So I crown the ram, though it lacks reason, with green flowers and dedicate it, Wolf of Hagia: it is not right to scorn the gifts of the gods.
XIX. Balthasar Richardus of Alsfeld.

units.la: Et tibi laureolam solenni confero ritu, Indole, cognomen qui bene, Dives habes. Hoc artis pretium vigilatorumq; laborum: His patet ad summum janua prima bonum.
units.tr: I bring a little laurel to you in solemn rite, you who have a good name and are rich in talent. This is the reward of skill and of watchful labours: by these the first door opens to the highest good.
XX. Theophilus Faber of Marburg.

units.la: Cultor amansq; Dei (namq; hoc tibi lotio nomen Sacra dedit) Fabrici, te mea Musa vocat. Virtutis sectare viam, comitabitur illam, Ingrediare, labor: progrediaris, amor. Emenso continget honos, lætusq; triumpus Hoc tibi, quam tribuo, laurea bacca monet.
units.tr: Worshipper and lover of God (for the sacred washing has given you this name), my Muse calls you, Faber. Pursue the way of virtue: labour will accompany you as you enter it, and love will carry you forward. Honour will come to you when the course is finished, and the joyful triumph; this laurel berry, which I give you, foretells it.
XXI. Christian Werner of Sontra.

units.la: Quod meruit doctrina tua ingeniosaq; virtus, Sertum do tibi docte Christiane. Quid sine re tituli? sine factis nomina vana? Et re sis maneasq; Christianus [?].
units.tr: Because your learning and gifted virtue have earned it, I give you a garland, learned Christian. What are titles without substance, or names without deeds? Be a Christian in truth, and remain one.
XXII. Nicolaus Crato of Marburg.

units.la: Huc Crato docte: Te vocat ordo: Te manet hujus Gloria serti, Quod tibi nullo Marcceat ævo, Et tibi Christus Verus Apollo Numine dexter Assit [?] amico.
units.tr: Come hither, learned Crato: the order calls you. The glory of this wreath awaits you, which will never wither in any age, and may Christ, the true Apollo, stand at your side with favouring divinity as a friend.

units.la: Constat & aeterna positum lege istud habetur: Ultima cunctarum rerum est perfectio finis. Finis ait, pater ille Sophûm, dat nomina rebus. Integer est à fine dies, non Solis ab ortu Integer, extremum, est, quem punctum terminat, orbis. Et tu ringere adhuc, Roslere, quod ultimus orbem Persicus hunc, obliqua trahens vestigia ponè: Et numerus numerum complex, nihilominus æquum Prorsus cum primo & medio sortitus honorem? Quin ades, & quæ deposuit tibi praemia apud me Musa, auferto, paris capiti gestamen honoris.
units.tr: It is also settled by an eternal law and held as fixed: the final perfection is the end of all things. The end, says that father of the wise, gives names to things. A day is whole from its end, not whole from the rising of the sun; the extremity is whole, the point that bounds the circle. And do you still ask, Roslere, why the Persian, drawing his tracks obliquely behind him, [stands last]? Or does the number that embraces number obtain an honour equal in every way to the first and the middle? Come, take the badge of honour that the Muse has set aside for you with me, for an equally worthy head.

units.la: EXHORTATIO AD JUVENES ET Studiosos cum voto.
units.tr: EXHORTATION TO YOUNG MEN AND STUDENTS, WITH A PRAYER.

units.la: ORnati juvenes, spes ô non parva virorum, Laurea collata hæc vobis reverenter habetor. Pro se quisq; decus partum virtute tuetor.
units.tr: Adorned young men, O hope of men, not small, this laurel conferred upon you is held in reverence. Each for himself I guard the honour won by virtue.

units.la: Vos verò reliqui, cunctos florere per annos Qui cupitis, juvenes, & honoris in arce locari, O fugite exosi pigra desidis otia vitæ, Et vires, omnesq; illuc contendite nervos, Ut crescente ævo vobis sapientia crescat: Qnod[?] faxit, precor, omne Deus trinunus in ævum.
units.tr: But you others, young men, who wish to flourish through all the years and to be set in the citadel of honour, flee, and hate the lazy idleness of a sluggish life. Strain your strength and all your sinews toward that goal, so that wisdom may grow in you as your age grows. May the triune God grant this, I pray, for ever.

units.la: Carmine acta sunt gratia Deo, Principibus, & auditoribus.
units.tr: Set down in verse. Thanks be to God, to the princes and to the hearers.
THE END.
